La historia contará que, con él como capitán y líder futbolístico, los portugueses fueron campeones de Europa, bicampeones de la Nations League y ganaron títulos cuando era algo que nunca antes habían vivido. 

Máximo goleador histórico. Máximo asistente histórico. Máximo anotador histórico del fútbol de selecciones. Máximo goleador de las Eurocopas. Máximo goleador portugués en Copas del Mundo. Gracias por tanto, Cristiano.

India’s Defence Exports Have Outgrown Its Public Account of Their Risks
India’s legal and diplomatic exposure over Gaza rests on a widening gap between the military relationship it is building with Israel and the evidence it publishes about the consequences. At the BRICS summit on 12 September 2026, New Delhi endorsed language condemning starvation as a method of warfare and opposing the forced displacement of Palestinians. Its defence partnerships nevertheless continued to develop through procurement, manufacturing and exports. Those activities do not, by themselves, establish complicity in unlawful conduct. They do require an explanation of how India evaluates the risks attached to particular recipients and transactions. The governing problem is accountability: the deeper the industrial relationship becomes, the less persuasive a general assurance about export controls becomes without records showing what authorities knew, what they examined and what restrictions they enforced.

BRICS language increases the burden of explaining export decisions
The BRICS New Delhi Declaration of 12 September 2026 placed India’s concern for Palestinian civilians in a collective institutional document. That commitment matters because New Delhi also endorsed closer defence cooperation with Israel through the bilateral “Special Strategic Partnership”. The relevant question is how the government applies the civilian-protection concerns it has formally endorsed when deciding whether military assistance should proceed.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s joint statement with Israel identified joint development, joint production and technology transfer in defence. These arrangements serve India’s domestic manufacturing ambitions while deepening relationships with Israeli suppliers. They also extend the range of decisions requiring scrutiny beyond purchasing a finished weapon: industrial cooperation creates continuing choices about components, production support and the conditions attached to their provision.

The Palestinian Foreign Ministry welcomed the BRICS declaration but called for practical and concrete steps. For India, an immediate test lies within its own administrative responsibilities: whether the government can show that its export decisions incorporate a substantive assessment of the risks described in the declaration. Diplomatic language becomes harder to defend when the decision records necessary to assess its implementation remain inaccessible.

The shipment figures demand scrutiny, not a shortcut to liability
The quantities in Amnesty International’s Made in India, published on 30 July 2026, make transaction-level examination necessary. Amnesty examined 2,596 shipments from India to Israel between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including 564,970 explosive-ordnance parts and 390,516 small-arms components. Its findings included 1,000 rounds of 155mm high-explosive artillery ammunition supplied by Munitions India to Elbit Systems and 120 mortar launchers of 81mm calibre supplied by Advanced Weapons and Equipment India in February 2024.

Amnesty identified nine exporters, including three state-owned companies: Munitions India, Advanced Weapons and Equipment India, and India Optel. Those findings increase the importance of examining government involvement. They do not eliminate the need to distinguish the legal status of each enterprise, the authority behind each decision and the subsequent destination of particular goods.

The commercial relationship is substantial in its own right. According to SIPRI’s figures for 2021–25, Israel supplied 15 per cent of India’s imports of major arms, while India received 29 per cent of Israel’s exports in that category. These shares establish a significant defence relationship. They do not measure the contribution of Indian exports to particular operations in Gaza, and they cannot substitute for evidence of operational use.

The distinction between categories also matters. Amnesty’s shipment analysis encompasses ammunition, parts and components; SIPRI’s figures concern major arms. A narrow measure of major weapons cannot resolve allegations about goods outside that category. Equally, a customs entry establishes neither the unlawfulness of the recipient’s subsequent conduct nor the supplier’s knowledge of it.

Joint manufacturing creates decisions that survive the original contract
Adani Elbit Advanced Systems’ Hyderabad venture illustrates the industrial transmission mechanism. The dossier describes production associated with the Hermes 900 drone, a model operated by the Israeli military over Gaza. The relevant legal inquiry concerns what the Indian venture supplied, to whom, under which conditions and with what knowledge. The shared platform name provides a reason to investigate those questions; it does not answer them.

The November 2025 memorandum on co-development and co-production institutionalised further cooperation between the defence establishments. As production relationships develop, the original contract date becomes an incomplete explanation for later conduct. Each subsequent delivery, amendment or support decision must be considered against the information available when that decision was taken.

A contract signed before 7 October 2023 can explain the origin of an obligation between commercial parties. It cannot establish that every later performance decision received an adequate risk assessment. For the transactions identified by Amnesty, a defensible examination would reconstruct the sequence of warnings, approvals and deliveries, then determine whether the relevant authorities reconsidered their position as information changed.

The Genocide Convention’s prevention obligation also makes practical influence relevant. Whether a supplier can restrict deliveries, enforce conditions or withhold support depends on the actual contractual and institutional arrangements. The dossier does not establish India’s transaction-specific leverage. That evidentiary gap calls for the relevant records, rather than an assumption that commercial importance either guarantees influence or leaves the supplier powerless.

Prevention duties arise before the evidence proves complicity
India ratified the Genocide Convention on 27 August 1959. The distinction between prevention and complicity is therefore consequential. Under the ICJ’s judgment of 26 February 2007, the duty to take preventive action arises when a state knows, or should normally know, of a serious risk of genocide. The required conduct depends on reasonably available means and the capacity to influence the actors concerned.

The same ICJ judgment sets a more demanding knowledge requirement for complicity: awareness of the principal perpetrator’s specific genocidal intent was at least necessary. It left unresolved whether an accomplice must also share that intent. An assessment of Indian assistance must preserve those distinctions. Failure to establish complicity would not, by itself, demonstrate that authorities adequately discharged a preventive duty.

Article 16 of the International Law Commission’s state-responsibility articles and commentary introduces another inquiry: assistance connected to an internationally wrongful act, with the requisite knowledge and contribution. The commentary addresses assistance intended to facilitate the act and actually contributing to it. A legally serious allegation must identify that conduct and connection; general awareness of the war cannot fill every evidentiary gap.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal’s assertion on 31 July 2026 that India possesses a “robust legal and regulatory framework” consequently answers only part of the question. A framework establishes the existence of controls. Assessing compliance requires evidence of their application to the transactions under examination, including the information considered and the reasons for proceeding.

Israel’s assurances must be tested against the obligations India retains
India’s Article IX reservation to the Genocide Convention requires consent for submitting disputes to the ICJ in each case. It concerns jurisdiction and should be analysed separately from substantive obligations. Likewise, India’s absence from the Arms Trade Treaty’s participant list prevents treating that treaty’s export provisions as obligations binding India as a state party. Neither point resolves the application of other international duties.

The ICJ’s 19 July 2024 advisory opinion adds a separate external constraint. It identifies obligations concerning non-recognition and non-assistance in maintaining Israel’s unlawful presence in the occupied Palestinian territory. Applying that reasoning to an Indian transaction requires an examination of what the transaction supported. The identity of an Israeli purchaser alone cannot establish the prohibited connection.

State-owned exporters also require a precise attribution analysis under the International Law Commission’s framework. Ownership does not automatically make every commercial act attributable to India. The inquiry concerns legal functions, instructions and control, while the government’s own approval decisions remain separately examinable. This distinction prevents both an unsupported allegation of comprehensive state responsibility and an equally unsupported claim that an enterprise’s corporate form settles the issue.

For Israeli recipients and Indian authorities, end-use assurances matter only to the extent that they address the identified risks and can be tested. The SCOMET licences and associated conditions described in the dossier are therefore central evidence. Their confidentiality leaves the public unable to determine whether safeguards were specific, whether compliance was checked, or whether reported concerns altered subsequent decisions.

Over the next two years, the cost will follow the decisions left unexplained
The ICJ’s order of 21 May 2026 sets 22 November 2027 for South Africa’s Reply and 22 May 2029 for Israel’s Rejoinder. These are procedural deadlines, not judgment dates. Over the next 12–24 months, India’s decisions will therefore continue to require justification without the convenience of a completed merits determination. Waiting for that outcome would leave the preventive-duty question unanswered.

For the companies identified in Made in India, an adequate record would separate lawful industrial activity from assistance alleged to support unlawful conduct. For Indian authorities, contemporaneous assessments would demonstrate what they knew and why they acted. If those records exist but remain withheld, the immediate cost is reduced public confidence in the government’s explanation. If they do not exist, the difficulty is more substantial: later statements cannot reconstruct the reasoning that should have informed the original decisions.

The BRICS declaration and the Special Strategic Partnership have already established India’s chosen diplomatic and industrial direction. The remaining choice concerns how that direction is governed. Publishing reasoned assessments, providing appropriate scrutiny of sensitive records and demonstrating that restrictions are enforceable would make the policy defensible on evidence. Leaving those questions unresolved transfers the burden to Indian exporters, public authorities and citizens who are asked to accept an account of the trade’s consequences that they cannot examine. -

The optics of former HOS or high-ranking public officials seeking medical treatment abroad and featured in promotional materials for foreign health centers highlight recurring structural and political dynamics in domestic infrastructure development. The viral promotional video from Krishna Shalby Hospital in Ahmedabad, India, featuring General Abdulsalami Abubakar after his total knee replacement surgery,ignited a controversial toxic reaction and polarized national debate on the legacy of public infrastructure and medical tourism.

Core Implications for Infrastructure Development:

 Lack of Elite "Skin in the Game": When decision-makers and political elites have access to foreign alternatives for essential services (such as healthcare and education), the incentive to invest in and maintain domestic public infrastructure diminishes. Because leaders do not directly rely on local hospitals, the institutional drive to fix systemic issues remains low.
 Economic Capital Flight: Outbound medical tourism drains foreign exchange reserves. Millions of dollars leave the domestic economy annually to fund medical care in regions like South Asia, Europe, and the Middle East—capital that could otherwise fund local medical research, equipment acquisition, and facility upgrades.

 Brain Drain and Capacity Erosion: Persistent underinvestment in domestic medical facilities encourages top medical professionals, surgeons, and nurses to migrate to countries with better working conditions and compensation. This perpetuates a cycle where domestic facilities lack specialized expertise.
 The Irony of Promotion: High-profile figures appearing in advertisements for foreign hospitals highlights a shift where domestic governance failures inadvertently serve as marketing material for foreign healthcare brands, signaling a vote of non-confidence in home-country facilities.

 Public Trust Deficit: 
Beyond physical infrastructure, the practice deepens public cynicism regarding governance. Citizens view the contrast between public service promises and private choices as a reflection of broken accountability mechanism

Key Financial & Operational Highlights

Assets Under Management (AUM): Stood at INR 8,001 crores, representing a robust growth of 61% YoY and 13% QoQ.

Profitability: Profit After Tax (PAT) grew to INR 95 crores (up 59% YoY and 16% QoQ), driven by organic profitability and operating leverage.

Return Metrics: Return on Average AUM held steady at 5.05%. Return on Average Equity (ROE) stood at 21.20%, despite a large capital infusion from the IPO.

User & Customer Base: Registered users grew 33% YoY to 74.6 million, while total served customers increased 26% YoY to 12.25 million.

Disbursements: Reached INR 3,812 crores, up 37% YoY. Growth is deliberately slower than AUM growth as repeat customers transition to longer loan tenures.

Balance Sheet Strength: Strengthened significantly following the May 2026 IPO. Net worth grew to INR 2,245 crores. Capital adequacy in the NBFC subsidiary rose sharply to 40.2% from 25.3% in the previous quarter.

Asset Quality & Underwriting Discipline

Credit Cost Improvement: Dropped significantly to 6.80% of average AUM, down from 7.02% in Q4 FY26 and 8.85% in Q1 FY26. The management maintained its guidance for a 15% total reduction in credit costs.

NPA & Coverage Metrics: Gross NPA stood range-bound at 2.25%, Net NPA at 0.36%, and Collection Efficiency at 96.82%. Provisioning remains highly conservative with Stage-3 ECL coverage at 84.1% and Stage-2 coverage at 80.4%.

Dynamic Risk Actions: Driven by early warning signals, the company paused lending across 450 pin codes in the previous quarter. Following re-evaluation and improving data trends, 40% (180 pin codes) have been safely reopened.

Industry Divergence: While headline industry metrics look calm, beneath the surface stress is building in small-ticket loans and over-leveraged borrowers across the industry. Kissht is tightening underwriting for specific segments, such as salaried profiles displaying a lack of fresh EPFO credits and highly volatile self-employed accounts.

Corporate Strategy & Product Trajectory

Shift to High-Quality Borrowers: Total income fell by 249 basis points over the quarter as a share of average AUM. This is a deliberate strategy to acquire safer, lower-risk customers who are priced lower, improving asset quality and retaining long-term value.

Off-Book Lending Expansion: The off-book AUM share increased from 49.7% to 53.6%, shifting the asset funding split to 46:54 (On-Book vs Off-Book) across more than 45 lending partners.

Loan Against Property (LAP): The tech-enabled LAP business grew to an AUM of INR 617 crores (7.7% of total AUM) across 101 branches in 8 states. LAP utilizes AI-validated valuations and model-based underwriting.

 Backed by cross-selling to existing personal loan clients, branches are breaking even in just 7 to 8 months, with the business expected to achieve overall breakeven by Q3.

Mutual Fund Distribution: The company secured an AMFI registration to expand capabilities into mutual fund and SIP distribution, opening a new fee-income pipeline alongside current insurance products.

Future Outlook & Cost of Funds

Margin & Funding Cost Improvements: Incremental borrowing cost is trending down, with a single Q1 debt raise executed at 12.9% (150 bps lower than the average FY26 borrowing cost).

 Management guides for a minimum 100 bps reduction in overall cost of borrowing, mainly taking effect in H2 FY27.

Growth Guidance: Confident in over-achieving the previously issued full-year AUM growth guidance of upwards of 40%, given the strong 13% QoQ start.

Potential areas: efficient drivetrains, transmissions, engine systems, electrification and precision components.

 3. Electrification + power electronics:
  → Sona BLW Precision Forgings

CAFE-driven electrification can increase content around motors, electronics, sensors, controllers, lighting and connected systems.

 4. Battery ecosystem:
  → Exide Industries

The opportunity is broader than BEVs: hybrids and electrified auxiliaries also require additional electrical/battery content. 

 5. Lightweighting:
  → Steel Strips Wheels
  → ASK Automotive
  → Jindal Aluminium
Less vehicle weight = lower energy requirement. This matters for both ICE and EVs, making lightweighting a powertrain-agnostic CAFE theme.

 6. Thermal management / HVAC:
  → Subros
  → Varroc Engineering
Efficient HVAC becomes increasingly relevant because every reduction in auxiliary energy consumption helps overall vehicle efficiency.

👉 So the CAFE story is not simply: ICE → EV. It is potentially: ICE → Efficient ICE → Hybrid → EV, with electronics, software, lightweight materials, thermal systems and power electronics gaining importance across the transition.

Former Head of State General Abdulsalami Abubakar’s treatment at an Indian hospital has sparked fresh reactions online, with Nigerians questioning the state of healthcare infrastructure and specialist medical services in the country.

Abdulsalami underwent total knee replacement surgery at Krishna Shalby Hospital in Ahmedabad, India. The Shalby hospital group has since highlighted his treatment in its promotional material, drawing renewed attention to the fact that a former Nigerian Head of State received specialised care outside the country.

The development has triggered discussions about why Nigerians, including prominent public figures, continue to seek specialised medical treatment abroad and whether Nigeria has invested enough in the facilities, equipment and specialist capacity needed to provide comparable care locally.

The debate is particularly significant because Abdulsalami served as Nigeria’s Head of State and, as reactions online show, his treatment abroad has become a reference point for wider frustrations about the country’s healthcare system.

The concerns are not limited to social media. Healthcare stakeholders in Nigeria recently called for sustainable financing, stronger public-private partnerships and improved regulation to address persistent gaps in primary healthcare delivery.

At the same time, the National Health Insurance Authority says ongoing reforms are expanding access to healthcare and improving health financing, showing that the debate also comes amid efforts to strengthen the sector.

For many Nigerians, however, the question remains: why should advanced medical care still require travelling abroad when the country has produced generations of highly trained medical professionals?

A High Court of the Federal Capital Territory in Maitama has ordered Jordan Ezenwo Nyesom-Wike, son of FCT Minister Nyesom Wike, to produce his American passport in court as hearing continued in a $2.1 million land-related suit.

Justice Sylvanus Oriji issued the order on Tuesday after the claimants’ counsel, Hamza Dantani, asked Jordan to produce the passport during cross-examination.

Jordan told the court that he was outside Nigeria on September 26, 2025, and that he travelled using his American passport. He said he could produce it if required, prompting the application for the court to order its production. The judge granted the request and adjourned the case until Wednesday.

The suit, marked CV/008/2026, was filed by Safwan Garba GY and GY Global Oil and Gas Nigeria Limited.

The claimants allege that Jordan agreed to help facilitate the acquisition of 30 hectares of land in Katampe and another 30 hectares in Guzape and demanded $2.1 million in facilitation fees. They allege that $2 million was meant for his father, while $100,000 was for Jordan.

They further allege that the money was delivered on September 26, 2025, but that the land was not secured and the money was not refunded.

Jordan has denied the allegations and adopted his statement on oath in court. His defence disputes the claimants’ account of the alleged transaction and says he was outside Nigeria on the date they identified for the payment.

The court has not made a final determination on the allegations, and the case remains ongoing.

Entry of Adani, RIL Welcome in Aluminium, Says Vedanta Chief

Will aid M&As in the sector, adds Agarwal

The Core Statement
Entry of the Adani Group and Reliance Industries into the aluminium sector will intensify competition and improve efficiency in the industry, Vedanta Chairman Anil Agarwal said, adding that the emergence of more players could eventually create room for mergers and acquisitions

Agarwal said the domestic aluminium industry currently has three major primary producers — Vedanta, Hindalco Industries and National Aluminium Company (Nalco)

"We welcome competition. Competition makes you more efficient," Agarwal said in an interview with FE. He said the entry of large business groups would bring greater competition into the sector, while over the longer term could lead to consolidation

Up for a Challenge — Key Points
The three primary producers of aluminium are Vedanta, Hindalco Industries and National Aluminium Company (Nalco)

Around 90% of production capacity is currently dominated by Vedanta and Hindalco

Vedanta is targeting aluminium capacity of around 6 MT in the next three years

Agarwal's Quotes
"We welcome competition. Whoever is efficient will survive"

"For now we are not pursuing any semiconductor ambition"

New Entrants' Plans
Adani Enterprises, along with UAE-based International Resources Holding, has announced an $11.5 billion integrated aluminium project in Odisha, comprising a 4 million tonne alumina refinery, a 2 million tonne aluminium smelter and a 1 million tonne downstream manufacturing park

Reliance Industries, meanwhile, has purchased tender documents for the Karlapat bauxite block in Odisha, which has attracted interest from several large industrial groups

Vedanta's Own Expansion Plans
Agarwal said Vedanta would continue to expand its aluminium business despite the entry of new players: "We have our plan. We are increasing our capacity"

Vedanta is targeting aluminium capacity of around 6 million tonne (MT) in the next three years, and 10 million tonne over 5-7 years, compared to 3 MT currently

"Whoever is efficient will survive," Agarwal said, adding that competition would force companies to improve productivity and costs

He said the emergence of more players could eventually lead to mergers as the industry evolves

The aluminium expansion is part of a broader $25 billion investment programme that Vedanta plans to undertake over the next three to five years across its businesses — spending will cover aluminium, oil & gas, zinc, steel, power and other businesses

"We are investing $25 billion in the next three to five years," Agarwal said. The group plans to fund the expansion through internal accruals, debt and asset recycling

At the same time, he said, the parent company would be brought to zero net debt within three years; debt at parent company level is at around $5 billion now, compared to $10 billion four years ago

Other Business Lines
Oil and gas: production could rise to around 500,000 barrels per day over the next three years from 300,000 barrels, with about $4 billion of investment planned

Zinc production is targeted at around 2 million tonne in two years, while silver output is expected to rise to 1,500 tonne

Group is also expanding its fertiliser, steel and power businesses

Power generation capacity could rise from around 4,000 MW currently to 12,000 MW, while the group is also looking at nuclear power

"We are looking at all the critical metals," Agarwal said, as Vedanta expands into critical minerals through exploration, mining and recycling

On Timelines & Semiconductor Plans
Timelines for critical-mineral projects would vary significantly: "Some projects can happen in one year, some will take three to five years," he said, adding that exploration was fundamental to building the country's domestic resource base

Agarwal also said the group currently has no plan to pursue semiconductor activity: "For now we are not pursuing any semiconductor ambition," indicating that Vedanta was focused on scaling its existing businesses

The group had earlier pursued a semiconductor foray in partnership with Foxconn

He said India needed to accelerate mineral exploration and production to reduce its dependence on imports — a stronger ecosystem of smaller exploration companies and startups, he said, would help identify deposits that could subsequently be developed by larger mining companies

Core Theme
The statement assumes significance because the primary aluminium sector has so far largely operated as a duopoly, with around 90% production capacity dominated by Vedanta and Hindalco Industries — the entry of Adani and RIL, backed by an $11.5 billion project and a bauxite block bid respectively, marks a structural shift that Agarwal, rather than resisting, has chosen to frame as a spur to efficiency, while simultaneously deploying $25 billion of Vedanta's own across aluminium, oil & gas, zinc, power and critical minerals to defend and grow its position, all while steering clear of the semiconductor ambitions it once pursued with Foxconn.

ESDS SOFTWARE SOLUTION LTD — Q1 FY27 INVESTOR ANALYSIS

Earnings Conference Call | 25 September 2026
ESDS Software Solution's Q1 FY27 call presents a business at an important transition point: the existing cloud, SaaS and managed-services business continues to grow steadily, while the company is preparing for a much larger AI/GPU infrastructure revenue cycle from Q3 FY27 onward.

The most important part of the call is therefore not the 7.3% Q1 revenue growth. It is the potential change in the revenue mix as 8,200 B300 GPUs for the Sharon AI factory, additional domestic GPU capacity, and a >50,000-GPU international pipeline begin moving toward commercial deployment.

1. Q1 FY27 — KEY NUMBERS

MetricQ1 FY27YoYRevenue from Operations₹133.66 Cr+7.28%Total Income₹135.17 Cr+7.5%EBITDA₹55.9 Cr—EBITDA Margin~42%—PBT₹36.47 Cr+5.1%PAT₹29.28 Cr+14.0%

Management described the quarter as one of steady, disciplined growth, with customer demand continuing across its three business verticals.
The CFO also clarified that Q1 revenue was 20.2% lower sequentially because Q4 FY26 included a significant one-time technical-design-services revenue contribution from a subsidiary.
Important distinction
The Q1 sequential decline therefore should not automatically be interpreted as deterioration in the underlying business.
The FY26 technical design revenue associated with the Sharon AI project was a milestone-based service and management explicitly said it was one-time; GPU revenue from the underlying deployment is expected from Q3 FY27.
2. WHAT ESDS ACTUALLY DOES
Management divides the business into three verticals:
1. Infrastructure-as-a-Service — IaaS
Cloud infrastructure
GPU infrastructure
Co-location
2. Software-as-a-Service — SaaS
Swaraj Cloud
Software products running on the Swaraj Cloud platform
3. Managed Services
Managing customers' cloud environments
Managing AI factories
Human-led technology/operational services
The company's strategy is to bundle these services rather than sell isolated products. Management explicitly said it prefers customers that take a combination of services because this creates greater customer dependence on the ESDS ecosystem.
3. Q1 REVENUE MIX
The Q1 FY27 revenue split was:
SegmentRevenue ContributionIaaS51.0%Managed Services31.31%SaaS17.55%
This is significant because the company is already predominantly an infrastructure business.
However, the composition of Managed Services needs careful interpretation.
FY26's unusually high Managed Services revenue was partly driven by the ₹85 Cr technical design service for the Sharon AI factory. Management said the business is now shifting toward IaaS revenue as the actual GPU infrastructure becomes operational.

4. THE SHARON AI DEAL — THE BIGGEST NEAR-TERM CATALYST

This is the central issue discussed during the call.

ESDS is supporting a large AI factory in Sydney involving approximately:

8,200 B300 GPUs

Management expects the AI factory to go live around early November 2026, with revenue beginning from Q3 FY27.

The earlier September target was delayed by roughly 1–1.5 months.

Contract structure

The GPUs are being deployed through the Sharon AI/GreenSquare ecosystem.

Management said:

The ESDS-Sharon contract is locked for 7 years
The customer contract is also locked
GPU prices may increase, but the contracted customer revenue is fixed at the agreed rate

Sharon AI has subsequently signed additional AI-factory deals

This gives ESDS a relatively long contractual period for the initial AI factory, although the economics after the seven-year period remain uncertain.
5. POTENTIAL GPU REVENUE ECONOMICS

Management said industry billing rates for advanced GPUs are currently around:

$5–$6 per GPU per hour
and ESDS expects to bill the Sharon customer in a similar range.
If all 8,200 GPUs were operational continuously at $5/hour, the simple theoretical gross billing would be:

8,200 × $5 × 24 × 365 ≈ $359 million/year

At $6/hour:

≈ $430 million/year

However, these are not company revenue guidance figures.
They are only mathematical illustrations based on management's stated GPU count and indicative hourly rate. Actual revenue would depend on deployment timing, utilization, billing structure, operating costs, capacity availability and contractual terms.
Management itself has explicitly declined to provide FY27/FY28 revenue or profit guidance.
6. CUSTOMER ADVANCE — A VERY IMPORTANT POINT
ESDS disclosed approximately:
₹1,100–1,200 Cr customer advance
related to the Sharon AI order.
Management confirmed that this advance is associated with the same Sharon AI contract and will be amortized monthly over the contract period once the GPU deployment becomes operational.
This is strategically important because it reduces the amount of upfront capital ESDS needs to fund the deployment.
7. GPU PIPELINE — >50,000 GPUs
The most aggressive statement on the call was that ESDS currently has a:

50,000+ GPU international funnel

Management said customers are waiting for supply and the company is working on determining where and how this capacity can be delivered.

This should be treated as a pipeline/funnel, not an order book.

That distinction is critical.

The company has not disclosed that all 50,000+ GPUs are contracted, funded or operational.

8. DOMESTIC ORDER BOOK

Management stated:

Domestic order book: ~₹3,000 Cr

with an approximate:

3-year duration

Management also indicated domestic business growth of approximately 30–40% CAGR, although this is a management statement rather than formal company guidance.

The international opportunity is described as materially larger than the domestic order book.

9. ESDS IS MOVING FROM "BUY GPU AFTER CUSTOMER" TO CAPACITY BUILDING

The company's strategy is changing.
Initially:
Customer → Contract → Procure GPU capacity
Going forward:

Build/secure capacity → approach RFS date → contract capacity

Management said it intends to build capacity through:

Partners

Own capital

Debt

Customer advances

IPO proceeds

and then contract the capacity closer to the required RFS date.

This could increase scalability, but it also introduces greater capital-allocation and utilization risk.

10. INDIA GPU CAPACITY

ESDS currently has a target to build approximately:

1,500 GPUs

Management expects deployment by January–February 2027, around Q4 FY27.

However, billing from the IPO-funded capacity is expected to begin around Q1 FY28, according to management.

This creates an important timing distinction:

Capacity deployment ≠ immediate revenue recognition.

11. CAPEX — THE BIG CHANGE IN FINANCIAL PROFILE

Management indicated FY27 capex of approximately:

₹1,500 Cr

and also referred to an additional ₹1,500 Cr of capex in FY27.

The funding sources mentioned include:

Customer advance

IPO proceeds

Partial debt

For the new India GPU capacity, management described a roughly 30%-30%-30% funding structure involving customer advance, lending and IPO proceeds.

This is a major change from a conventional asset-light software model.

12. THE ECONOMIC MODEL

The emerging AI-factory model can be simplified as:

Customer advance
↓
ESDS secures GPU/data-centre capacity
↓
GPU deployment
↓
AI compute rented to customer
↓
Long-duration contractual revenue
↓
GPU/capacity financing + operating costs
↓
PAT margin target of 15–20%

Management specifically stated that it is targeting 15–20% PAT margins on these types of deals and does not intend to work below that level.

This is a management target, not an achieved margin.

13. WHY THE GPU BUSINESS COULD SCALE WITHOUT A MASSIVE EMPLOYEE BASE

Current employee strength:

993

Management expects approximately 100 additional people from the Sharon deal but does not expect total employee count to rise materially above 1,000 because partners will provide personnel for parts of the AI-factory infrastructure.

This potentially creates operating leverage:

GPU capacity ↑ significantly
while
employee count ↑ relatively slowly

That is an important feature of the model if execution works as planned.

14. GPU SUPPLY IS CURRENTLY A CONSTRAINT

Management said GPU availability is already constrained, with delivery timelines extending:

4–6 months and sometimes 9 months

ESDS is attempting to accelerate delivery through its OEM/ODM and NVIDIA relationships.

Therefore, the bottleneck may not be customer demand.

It may be:

GPU supply + power + data-centre capacity + financing + deployment capability.

15. GPU ASSET LIFE
Management argues that NVIDIA GPUs can have an extended commercial life.
Its example:
A100/H100 — several years old
Still attracting customer demand

Older GPUs can migrate from AI labs to gaming, e-commerce, rendering and other workloads

Management estimates useful economic life of GPUs could extend to around:

8 years

This is management's view and should not be treated as independently verified asset-life guidance.

The important business implication is that GPU economics may not necessarily resemble traditional IT hardware depreciation.

16. INTERNATIONAL EXPANSION

ESDS does not intend to build only in India.

Management said it plans a combination of:

India

International data centres

Local partners

Countries with green/clean power availability

This is strategically relevant because AI factories require significant electricity.

Access to:

cheap + reliable + clean power

could become a competitive advantage.

17. NEW PRODUCT ECOSYSTEM
The company is building Swaraj Cloud, described by management as an AI autonomous sovereign cloud platform incorporating:
Compute

Storage

Networking

Databases

AI/GPU infrastructure

Cybersecurity

Managed services
Two new products were also launched:
Swaraj Garuda
Application performance monitoring and observability.
Swaraj Jatayoo
Database activity monitoring.
This supports the company's broader strategy of combining infrastructure with software and managed services.
18. CROSS-SELLING IS A CORE STRATEGY
ESDS does not want to be simply a GPU-rental company.
The preferred model is:
IaaS
+
SaaS
+
Managed Services
The customer therefore potentially buys:
Cloud → GPU → software → cybersecurity → database → monitoring → managed services.

Management explicitly stated that profitability is high in SaaS, while GPU/IaaS margins are also improving as the AI-factory business grows.

19. SEASONALITY

Management acknowledged that Q4 has historically been stronger.

The reason is partly the timing of AI-factory deployments and customer deliveries.

However, management expects seasonality to reduce over the next 2–3 years as more AI factories are delivered and billing becomes more evenly distributed across months.

Therefore:

Q1 FY27 +7.3% revenue growth

does not necessarily represent the expected growth profile once large AI factories begin contributing.

20. THE MOST IMPORTANT FINANCIAL TRANSITION
There are effectively two ESDS businesses emerging:
EXISTING BUSINESS

Cloud + SaaS + Managed Services

Steady growth
High margins
Recurring customers

↓

NEW BUSINESS

GPU Infrastructure + AI Factories

Large contracts
High upfront capital requirement
Long-duration contracts
Customer advances
Potentially large revenue scale

The second business could materially change the company's revenue trajectory, but it also changes the capital intensity and risk profile.

21. KEY CATALYSTS

1. Sharon AI 8,200-GPU deployment

Expected around early November/Q3 FY27.

2. 1,500-GPU India capacity

Targeted for Q4 FY27 deployment.

3. 50,000+ GPU funnel

Large potential international pipeline, subject to conversion into contracts.
4. ₹3,000 Cr domestic order book
Management says it has a three-year duration.

5. Customer advances

Large upfront advances can reduce funding requirements.

6. GPU pricing

Management expects GPU prices/rental rates to remain strong because of demand-supply imbalance.

7. Sovereign cloud

Swaraj Cloud can potentially increase SaaS contribution and cross-selling.

22. KEY RISKS

1. Execution risk

An 8,200-GPU AI factory is operationally complex.
Delays have already occurred: the original September timeline moved toward November.
2. GPU availability
Delivery timelines can extend up to 9 months.

3. Capital intensity

The planned capex is dramatically larger than the existing business scale.

4. Customer concentration

The Sharon AI project is currently extremely significant.

Management argues that customer advances and strong GPU demand reduce concentration risk, but this remains an important variable to monitor.

5. Contract renewal

The Sharon arrangement is described as a seven-year contract, but management itself acknowledged that what happens after seven years is uncertain.

6. GPU obsolescence
Management expects long useful lives, but GPU technology changes rapidly.
7. Pipeline conversion
50,000+ GPUs is a funnel, not booked revenue.
Conversion into signed contracts, advances and live capacity needs to be tracked.
8. Margin risk
Management targets 15–20% PAT margins for these GPU deals, but these margins have not yet been demonstrated at scale.

23. WHAT MATTERS MOST FROM Q3 FY27

The next few quarters are likely to be unusually important.

KPIWhat to watchSharon GPUs8,200 deploymentGo-liveEarly Nov / Q3 FY27GPU billingActual revenue commencementGPU utilizationActual vs contracted capacityRevenue/GPUActual realized economicsPAT marginTarget 15–20%Customer advancesGrowth and amortizationDomestic order book~₹3,000 CrInternational GPU funnel>50,000 GPUsIndia GPU capacity1,500 targetFY27 capex~₹1,500 Cr + additional capex referred toEmployee count~1,000SaaS contributionWhether it expandsCash flowCritical as capex accelerates

24. THE KEY INVESTOR QUESTION

The most important question is no longer simply:

"Can ESDS grow its cloud business?"

It is:

Can ESDS convert extraordinary GPU demand into high-return, long-duration infrastructure contracts without destroying capital efficiency?

The answer will depend on five variables:

GPU supply
× Customer advances
× Utilization
× Rental pricing
× Financing cost
If these remain favorable, the AI-factory business could operate with significant scale benefits.
If GPU procurement, financing or utilization deteriorates, the much larger capex requirement could materially change the risk profile.
25. MANAGEMENT'S FORWARD VIEW — WITHOUT COMPANY GUIDANCE
Management has explicitly not provided FY27/FY28 revenue or profit guidance.

Therefore, it would be inappropriate to convert the 50,000+ GPU funnel, $5–$6/hour indicative billing rates or 30–40% domestic CAGR comments into formal earnings estimates.

The company has instead provided operational milestones:

Sharon AI → ~8,200 GPUs

India → ~1,500 GPUs

International funnel → >50,000 GPUs

Domestic order book → ~₹3,000 Cr

GPU deal PAT-margin target → 15–20%

Seven-year Sharon contract

Q3/Q4 FY27 deployment ramp

These milestones are the appropriate framework for tracking execution.

26. ESDS BUSINESS MODEL — FROM CLOUD TO AI FACTORY

The company's evolution can be represented as:

Cloud Hosting
↓
Cloud + Managed Services
↓
Swaraj Cloud
↓
GPU Infrastructure
↓
AI Factory
↓
Global AI Compute Platform

The strategic opportunity is that ESDS could sit between:

GPU owners / data-centre partners

and

global AI companies / enterprises
while adding its own cloud, software, cybersecurity and managed-services layer.
27. INVESTOR DASHBOARD

Current business

Q1 Revenue: ₹133.7 Cr
Q1 PAT: ₹29.3 Cr
EBITDA Margin: ~42%
IaaS: 51%
Managed Services: 31.3%
SaaS: 17.55%

AI infrastructure opportunity

Sharon AI: 8,200 GPUs
GPU type: B300
Contract: 7 years
Indicative billing: $5–$6/GPU/hour
Domestic order book: ~₹3,000 Cr
Order-book duration: ~3 years
International GPU funnel: >50,000
Planned India GPUs: ~1,500
GPU-deal PAT target: 15–20%
Funding/capacity
Customer advance: ~₹1,100–1,200 Cr
FY27 capex referred to: ~₹1,500 Cr plus additional capex
Employees: 993
Expected employee count: around 1,000
BOTTOMLINE
ESDS Software Solution is entering a potentially transformational phase.

The existing business is already profitable, with Q1 FY27 revenue of ₹133.7 Cr, PAT of ₹29.3 Cr and approximately 42% EBITDA margin.

But the bigger story is the transition toward AI infrastructure and GPU-as-a-Service.

The immediate trigger is the 8,200-GPU Sharon AI factory, expected to begin contributing from Q3 FY27. Beyond that, management cites a >50,000-GPU international funnel, a ₹3,000 Cr domestic order book, and planned deployment of approximately 1,500 GPUs in India.

The opportunity is substantial, but so is the change in risk profile: ESDS is moving from a relatively asset-light technology-services model toward a much more capital-intensive AI-compute infrastructure model.

The next critical evidence will therefore come from actual GPU deployment, revenue recognition, utilization, customer advances, capex, financing costs and achieved PAT margins—rather than pipeline numbers alone.

The Q3 FY27 Sharon AI go-live is the key operational milestone to watch.

SCI completes 65 years, special ceremony to be held in Mumbai on October 2, Sonowal to be present!

Marine Tanks

Mumbai: The Shipping Corporation of India Limited (SCI) will celebrate its 65 years of glorious journey on October 2, 2026. According to the information, the ceremony will be held from 5 PM onwards at The Ballard Pier Downtown Experience Centre, Ballard Estate, Mumbai.

It may be noted that SCI was established on October 2, 1961, through the merger of Eastern Shipping Corporation and Western Shipping Corporation. The company started with 19 ships and, over a journey spanning more than six decades, has established itself as one of the leading institutions in Indian maritime transportation.

Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal will be the chief guest at the ceremony. Union Minister of State Shantanu Thakur and Nitesh Narayan Rane, Minister of Fisheries and Ports Development in the Maharashtra Government, along with other prominent people associated with the maritime sector, will also be present.

🚨 SUDARSHAN CHEMICAL: ACQUISITION MOVE

A new strategic acquisition step has been disclosed.

Sudarshan Chemical Industries has announced the execution of a Share Purchase Agreement (SPA).

🔎 WHAT IS AN SPA?

A Share Purchase Agreement is the contractual framework through which shares of a target company/business are acquired.

The announcement therefore represents a significant step in the acquisition process.

🏭 WHY THIS MATTERS

Sudarshan Chemical is using inorganic expansion as part of its broader business strategy.

An acquisition can potentially provide:

• New products
• New customers
• Geographic expansion
• Additional manufacturing capability
• Technology
• Synergies

📌 IMPORTANT

An SPA announcement should not automatically be treated as completed acquisition.

Investors need to track:

Signing → conditions → closing → integration → financial contribution

👀 WHAT TO WATCH

1️⃣ Target company/business
2️⃣ Purchase consideration
3️⃣ Stake acquired
4️⃣ Funding source
5️⃣ Closing conditions
6️⃣ Revenue/profit contribution
7️⃣ Synergies

**The agreement is the first major milestone.

The financial impact comes after completion and integration.**

Gautam Adani, four Adani Group companies and other individuals have settled proceedings with SEBI over alleged non-compliance with minimum public shareholding (MPS) requirements.

The companies involved are Adani Enterprises, Adani Power, Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone, and Adani Transmission, now known as Adani Energy Solutions. The proceedings originated from complaints received by SEBI in 2020, followed by an investigation and show-cause notices issued in 2024 and 2025.

The four company-director groups paid ₹37.05 lakh each, taking the combined settlement amount to ₹1.482 crore. The payments were made on August 26, 2026.

Importantly, the settlement was reached without the applicants admitting or denying the allegations. SEBI has now disposed of the proceedings covered by the settlement.

The case underlines why MPS requirements matter: listed companies are generally required to maintain at least 25% public shareholding, ensuring that a meaningful portion of ownership remains with public investors.

iCanFly Recognised as Best Emerging OTA Platform of the Year 2026 - Sri Lanka

iCanFly has been recognised as the Best Emerging OTA (Online Travel Agency) Platform of the Year 2026 - Sri Lanka at the Indian Travel & Technology Summit & Awards 2026, held on 25 September 2026 at Hyatt Regency, Gurugram (Delhi NCR), India.

According to the organisers, the recognition acknowledges iCanFly’s excellence, contribution and leadership within the travel and technology ecosystem.

iCanFly is a Sri Lankan digital travel platform offering travellers access to a growing range of services through its website and mobile app, including flight bookings, special student fares, hotel bookings and travel insurance. The platform is designed to bring key elements of the travel journey together in one place, making it easier for customers to search, compare and book travel services digitally.

The company continues to enhance its platform with a focus on convenience, choice and simplifying the overall booking experience for travellers.

The Indian Travel & Technology Summit & Awards 2026 brought together leaders and decision-makers from across the travel, tourism, hospitality and technology sectors.

The summit’s participants, speakers and panel representatives included organisations such as Google, MakeMyTrip, Cleartrip, ixigo/ConfirmTkt, https://t.co/ZypIST6EdY, Accenture Technology, RateHawk, TravClan, Radisson Hotels Group, Hilton, IHG Hotels & Resorts, Cinnamon Life, Thomas Cook India, SOTC Travel, IndiGo, Digi Yatra Foundation, World Bank Group, Siemens Energy India and Palo Alto Networks, among others.

The Summit was supported by the Ministry of Tourism and Culture, Government of India, along with Tourism Boards.

Commenting on the recognition, Nabeel Fuward, Managing Director of iCanFly, said:

“This recognition is an important milestone for iCanFly and reflects the effort our team has put into building a simpler and more accessible digital travel experience. We are grateful to our customers, partners and team for being part of this journey.”

Before KKR vs After KKR 
TLDR;
#QuestioningConvictionMuscle 

#CGPOWER #MAXHEALTH #POONAWALLA #MFSL #SBILIFE #DALBHARAT #HDFCBANK #COFFEEDAY #INDUSTOWER

9 investments. 9 different stories. 
9 convictions worth questioning.

“KKR exited” sounds like useful information.

But without knowing why KKR entered, what changed while it owned the stake, and why it eventually sold, it tells us surprisingly little.

The image shows the returns.
The stories are more interesting.

1. CGPOWER | The investment KKR never really chose

KKR did not enter CG Power as a conventional PE bet.

In September 2019, KKR’s credit entities ended up with ~10% of CG Power at ₹14.25/share by enforcing pledged shares against loans made to the promoter group.

And look at the situation then.

CG Power had just disclosed serious accounting and governance irregularities. 

Liabilities had been understated, related-party transactions were under investigation, operations were deteriorating and lenders were looking for a resolution.

So KKR’s “thesis” here was primarily credit recovery, not:
Power equipment is going to boom.

KKR sold during 2020.

Then Murugappa Group entered through Tube Investments, repaired the balance sheet, restored governance and rebuilt the operating business.

Today, the backdrop could barely look more different.

India is in another large transmission/grid-capex cycle, driven by electrification and renewable integration.

CG Power has also added an entirely new semiconductor adjacency through CG Semi, whose first facility started commercial production in 2026.

Post-KKR reference return: ~51x.

Questioning the conviction:
Can a terrible company situation temporarily hide a very good underlying industrial asset?

2. MAXHEALTH | Consolidation before healthcare became fashionable

KKR-backed Radiant moved on Max Healthcare in 2018.

The thesis was unusually explicit:
scale + consolidation + cost synergies + margin improvement + growing demand for quality healthcare.

The merger created one of India's largest hospital networks, with more than 3,200 beds at the time, and KKR specifically highlighted the ability to use the platform for further healthcare consolidation.

KKR eventually made roughly 5x and exited.

But that did not mean India's hospital runway had ended.

Max today operates 6,100+ beds, while large Indian hospital operators continued delivering >15% revenue and EBITDA growth in FY26 amid further capacity build-out.

Post-KKR: ~2.83x.

Questioning the conviction:
When PE has already made 5x, has the opportunity matured, or has the company merely moved from turnaround → scale → compounding?

P.S: I personally stay away from direct investments in healthcare sector.

3. POONAWALLA | Magma was originally a financial-inclusion bet

Go back to 2011.

Magma was not today's Poonawalla Fincorp.

It was an NBFC heavily exposed to rural and semi-urban India, financing commercial vehicles, construction equipment, tractors, cars and SMEs.

Around 80% of its branches were in rural/semi-urban markets.

I could not find a clean public KKR statement spelling out its exact thesis, but the contemporaneous investment documents make the likely thesis fairly clear:
underserved credit + branch expansion + product expansion + financial inclusion.

KKR exited around 2018 at roughly 2x.

Then the company itself changed.

New promoter. New balance sheet.
New distribution. New products. 
New underwriting architecture.

By FY26, Poonawalla Fincorp had ₹60,348 Cr AUM, up 69.4%, with a much broader mix across secured and unsecured products.

Post-KKR: ~2.68x.

Questioning the conviction:
In lending, what is the real moat?
Distribution? Cost of capital? 
Underwriting? Or the ability to reinvent all three?

4. MFSL | KKR explicitly bet on financialisation

KKR bought 9.95% of Max Financial in 2016 just after the Max Group demerger created a clean listed life-insurance vehicle.

KKR's rationale was explicit:
India's growth, increasing financial savings, and the resulting growth of the life-insurance industry.

That structural thesis largely played out.

But today's question is different.

IRDAI is now proposing another reset of insurance distribution economics, including tighter commission and expense structures.

Post-KKR reference: ~+120%.

Questioning the conviction:
If insurance penetration remains low but distribution economics change, who captures the next decade's value: bank, agent or platform?

5. SBILIFE | Distribution itself was an asset
KKR entered SBI Life in December 2016 at ₹460/share, shortly before its IPO.

The attraction was difficult to miss.

SBI Life combined a leading private insurer with access to the enormous SBI distribution network. 

Contemporary analysis highlighted its profitability, product mix and reach through SBI's banking franchise.

KKR subsequently monetised through multiple transactions.

Post-KKR reference: ~+77%.

Now the same industry faces a new question as regulators try to lower distribution costs.

Questioning the conviction:
In insurance, is a giant distribution network always an advantage, or does its value change when commissions themselves are regulated downward?

6. DALBHARAT | KKR bought cement when everyone could see oversupply

In 2010, Indian cement was dealing with massive capacity additions, falling utilisation and pricing pressure, particularly in southern India. Industry utilisation had already fallen sharply as new supply entered.

And KKR invested ₹750 Cr into Dalmia.

Why?
The money was explicitly meant for:
organic growth + inorganic growth + deleveraging.

Dalmia was restructuring itself into a focused cement platform, had reached 9 MTPA capacity and was planning another 10 MTPA of greenfield projects.

KKR eventually made 3.6x.

Post-KKR: ~+61%.

Questioning the conviction:
Is industry overcapacity always bearish?

Or can the weak part of a cycle actually be the best time for a low-cost player with capital to build capacity?

7. HDFCBANK | KKR wasn't just buying a mortgage lender

KKR invested in HDFC Ltd in early 2018.

But look at what the fresh capital was meant for:

→ maintain HDFC's stake in HDFC Bank
→ health-insurance opportunities
→ stressed real-estate assets
→ affordable housing
→ funding subsidiaries

It was effectively backing a capital-allocation platform, not merely a home-loan book.

Then came the NBFC liquidity crisis.

Years later came the HDFC Ltd + HDFC Bank merger.

KKR itself had already exited with roughly a 15% gain.

Post-KKR equivalent price return: ~+22%.

Questioning the conviction:
Was HDFC's historical moat the mortgage product itself, or the ecosystem, funding advantage and capital allocation around it?

That distinction matters even more after the merger.

8. COFFEEDAY | Right consumption thesis. Wrong balance-sheet outcome.

In 2010, KKR called Café Coffee Day a fast-growing retailer.

The consumer story was obvious.

India's organised retail market was expanding rapidly, CCD had built enormous brand recognition, and cafés were becoming part of urban India's changing consumption habits.

But KKR wasn't buying only a coffee shop.

The holding company also contained several other businesses, including real estate/infrastructure-related assets.

KKR monetised some shares at much higher prices, but remained invested while leverage and corporate complexity overwhelmed the consumer story.

Its eventual overall outcome was only around 1.2x.

Questioning the conviction:
Can you be completely right about the consumer trend and still lose because the capital structure is wrong?

Brand ≠ balance sheet.

9. INDUSTOWER | Telecom grew. The tower stock didn't compound accordingly.

KKR invested $250m in Bharti Infratel in 2008.
The setup was compelling.

India was adding telecom subscribers rapidly. Operators were expanding into new geographies. 

Sharing passive infrastructure allowed faster rollouts and better economics.

The tower model had significant operating leverage because each additional tenant could improve returns on an already-built asset.

KKR eventually made roughly 1.8x.

Yet the successor Indus Towers has delivered roughly flat-to-negative price returns from our exit reference, excluding substantial dividends.

Meanwhile the underlying infrastructure never became irrelevant.

Indus is still adding towers and co-locations, has 563,000 installed 5G BTSs, and its tenancy ratio stands around 1.62.

Questioning the conviction:
Can an industry experience exponential data growth while the infrastructure owner still delivers mediocre stock returns?

Absolutely.

Demand growth ≠ shareholder returns.
And that connects all nine stories.

KKR exiting is an event.
It is not an investment thesis.

PE investors have fund lives, return hurdles and liquidity constraints.

They also often own meaningful blocks.

So exits commonly happen through multiple block/bulk/open-market transactions, sometimes spread across months or years.

More importantly, KKR's investment objective and your investment objective can be completely different.

The better questions are:

Why did they enter?
What changed while they were there?
Why are they exiting?

And which part of the original thesis still has runway after they leave?

That, to me, is a much better way to exercise the #QuestioningConvictionMuscle than blindly following “smart money.”

🚨 KALYAN JEWELLERS JUMPS 2.5%, TOPS MIDCAP GAINERS: UBS RETAINS ₹900 TARGET

Kalyan Jewellers India shares gained around 2.5% to ₹578 in early trade on September 29, outperforming a weak broader market after UBS reiterated its Buy rating on the jewellery retailer.

🔹 Stock price: ~₹578
🔹 Early gain: ~2.5%
🔹 Previous close: ₹564
🔹 2026 YTD gain: ~19%
🔹 Market cap: ~₹59,600 Cr
🔹 UBS target price: ₹900
🔹 Implied upside from previous close: ~60%

The ₹900 target and Buy rating are UBS's estimates, not our recommendation.

WHY IS UBS POSITIVE? 📈

Following interactions with Kalyan Jewellers' management, UBS highlighted expectations of stronger growth during the second half of the current financial year despite a high base.

Key factors highlighted include:

🔹 Stronger H2 growth outlook
🔹 Continued aggressive store expansion
🔹 Visibility from gold savings schemes
🔹 Capital-light expansion through the FOCO model
🔹 Long-term opportunity from organised jewellery gaining market share

GOLD PRICES REMAIN AN IMPORTANT VARIABLE 🪙

Management indicated that elevated gold prices are affecting customer segments differently.

Higher gold prices can influence:

🔹 Jewellery demand
🔹 Average ticket sizes
🔹 Consumer purchasing behaviour
🔹 Product mix

However, UBS believes Kalyan's growth can continue to be supported by network expansion and market-share gains.

AGGRESSIVE STORE EXPANSION 🏬

UBS had initiated coverage on Kalyan Jewellers earlier this month with the same ₹900 target.

The brokerage highlighted the company's franchise-owned, company-operated model as an important driver of capital-efficient expansion.

UBS also noted that Kalyan's pace of store additions has been nearly twice that of Titan.

GROWTH TRACK RECORD 📊

According to UBS:

🔹 Revenue CAGR FY22-FY26: ~35%
🔹 Expected revenue CAGR over next 5 years: ~23%
🔹 Expected earnings CAGR over next 5 years: ~23%

The brokerage also estimates Kalyan trades at around 30x FY28 earnings, representing roughly a 45% discount to Titan.

KEY TAKEAWAY 📌

Kalyan Jewellers' move stands out because it came while the broader market was under pressure.

The UBS thesis is primarily built around continued store expansion, the capital-light FOCO model, market-share gains and expectations of strong revenue and earnings growth.

The stock's ~19% gain in 2026 also contrasts with the Nifty 50's double-digit decline over the same period.

WHAT TO WATCH 👀

H2 same-store sales growth, new store additions, franchise economics, margins and the impact of elevated gold prices on consumer demand will remain important operating monitorables.

Execution becomes particularly important given the company's rapid network expansion and the growth expectations embedded in brokerage estimates.

ESDS Software Solution: a positive credit signal 

One development from today that ESDS investors shouldn’t overlook:

India Ratings has upgraded ESDS’s bank-facility ratings to:

→ Long-term: IND A / Stable
→ Short-term: IND A1

The upgrade indicates an improved assessment of the company’s credit profile.

What makes this interesting is the broader picture:

ESDS had already received a CRISIL upgrade earlier this month to A-/Positive / A2+
• FY26 operating income stood at ₹473 Cr, with PAT of ₹121 Cr
• CRISIL reported low adjusted debt/equity of 0.08x and interest coverage of 20.6x
• Cash & equivalents were around ₹1,200 Cr as of March 2026. 

But there is an important counterpoint:

Q1 FY27 was weak sequentially, with revenue and PAT declining QoQ. 

So I see today’s rating upgrade as a positive balance-sheet/credit-quality signal, not a reason to ignore execution risks.

For me, the key things to watch now are:

AI/cloud deployment → revenue growth → margins → cash generation → capex discipline.

India installed 8.2 GWh of grid batteries in the first half of 2026.

Nearly every cell inside them was imported.

Why does that matter?

Look at the demand side.
H1 2025: 98 MWh of battery storage installed.
H1 2026: 8.2 GWh.

That's 84 times in one year.
Crisil expects another 45 to 50 GWh to be commissioned across FY27 and FY28. Wood Mackenzie puts India's storage tender pipeline at 260 GWh.

Now the supply side.
In August, Wood Mackenzie counted 2 GWh of operational cell capacity in India. That's enough to meet less than 1% of the pipeline. Even with Exide's new 6 GWh line, which isn't in commercial production yet, domestic supply is a small fraction of what's coming.

So the gap gets filled by imports.
🔹 Li-ion battery imports in FY26: $4.7 bn, up 57%
🔹 Share from China: 83.6%

And this isn't just a trade deficit number. It shows up in P&Ls.

Chinese storage cell prices rose 22% in six months. Crisil says battery costs went from $50 to 55/kWh in 2025 to $70 to 75/kWh in 2026.

Developers usually buy batteries about a year after winning a bid. So projects won at 2025 tariffs are now paying 2026 prices. Crisil flags 12 GWh of capacity with weak returns.

When one country supplies your cells, it also sets your margins.

That's why local manufacturing matters.  For pricing power.

India has announced 226 GWh of cell capacity through 2035. 

Here's the part most people miss.
In July 2025, Beijing added LFP cathode technology to its restricted-export list. Taking it out of China now needs a licence.

On paper, that covers one material. On the ground, Indian companies are telling a very different story.

Amara Raja signed a licence with Gotion's European arm in 2024. It never moved. The company is now building its own tech, and its new-energy head says sharing is "largely discouraged by the Chinese government."

Then came the part that made me stop.

This week, Advait signed to buy up to 1 GWh of cells from China's Hithium. Back in January, Bloomberg reported that Hithium wouldn't license its LFP tech to Reliance. Reliance denied it.

So China will sell India the cell. Just not the recipe.

JSW has stopped waiting for it.

Last week, chairman Sajjan Jindal called the cell "the new oil" and said China will supply cells but won't share the know-how. His own estimate for building the technology in-house: one to two years, if things go well.

Also, JSW Projects and COEP Tech announced a battery R&D centre in Pune, with over ₹800 crore committed across two phases. Phase 1 will design and prototype lithium-ion and sodium-ion cells. Phase 2 is a validation centre able to produce cells from 100 to 600 Ah.

And Exide? Its 6 GWh plant was commissioned last week on SVOLT technology. But that deal was signed in March 2022, three years before the door closed.

Where India's own effort stands:
🔹 PLI ACC scheme: 40 GWh awarded, ~1.4 GWh operational, zero incentives paid as of Feb 2026
🔹 Ola Electric: 2.5 GWh operational, in-house technology
🔹 Amara Raja: first 2 GWh line targeted for 2027
🔹 Agratas (Tata): 20 GWh at Sanand, first equipment arrived this month, output in 2027

If the lock sits on the cathode, the materials layer is where it gets interesting:
🔹 Gujarat Fluorochemicals: supplying LiPF6 commercially since Dec 2025. LFP cathode final qualification expected by Q3 FY27
🔹 Himadri Speciality: 40,000 tpa LFP cathode in Phase I, first 2,000 tpa by Q3 FY27
🔹 Neogen Chemicals: ₹1,795 cr battery-chemicals capex, electrolyte production in H1 FY27

🔸 The other side: restricted is not banned, and licences can still be granted. Home-grown cells cost 25 to 40% more than imports. 

And China's wider controls on anode, cathode and cell-making equipment are only suspended, until 10 Nov 2026.

India can announce gigawatts. Buying the recipe is getting harder.

Why interest rates and earnings growth matter so much when judging index valuations.
To understand this more applicable way is to look at Nifty valuation is through the "equity risk premium" ! 
At around 19–20x PE, Nifty earnings yield is roughly 5–5.2%.
India’s 10-year bond yield is around 6–7%.
So purely on current yield, equities are not giving you any obvious premium over bonds, & the extra return has to come from future earnings growth.
If Nifty earnings grow 12–14% for the next few years, this can still work well because your earnings base keeps expanding, but if earnings growth drops to 6–8%, suddenly the present valuation starts looking far less attractive.

Srirangam, 1323. The year the temple emptied.

The Koyil Olugu is the chronicle the Ranganathaswamy temple kept of itself. It is the source for what follows. Not a modern reconstruction. The temple's own record of its own worst year. Malik Kafur had already been through the Tamil country in 1311 and robbed Srirangam. In 1323 Ulugh Khan came back.

The Koyil Olugu records 12,000 Srivaishnavas at Srirangam. It records that 11,250 of them were killed.

Before the killing started the priests got the utsava murti of Ranganatha out. They carried the deity into the forests of Kerala, then up into the hills at Tirupati, where it stayed. The sanctum at Srirangam stood empty for ~60 years.

Think about what that means as a fact of ordinary life. 3 generations of a temple town where the god was not at home. Children born, married and buried at Srirangam who never saw the deity in its own sanctum.

In 1371 the Vijayanagara commanders brought Ranganatha back and put the deity in its place. Srirangam is the largest functioning temple complex on earth. 156 acres. 7 concentric walls. 21 gopurams. It is not a ruin and it is not a museum, because the people who carried the deity out did not let it become one.

Go to Srirangam and stand in the sanctum. Then read the Koyil Olugu and work out what it cost to keep that sanctum occupied.

Pic: the Ranganathaswamy temple, Srirangam.

UAE–India: The Real Numbers Behind the $25 Billion Headline

The $25 billion is intent, not money already parked in India. UAE funds have already invested about $25 billion in total. Another $25 billion “in the near future,” with a long-term aim of $100 billion. That would take the stock from ~$25 billion toward ~$50 billion first, then higher if deals close. UAE is India’s 7th-largest FDI source, not the largest.⁠

Deals already named (these are real, not just talk): Emirates NBD’s about $3 billion majority stake in RBL Bank; Abu Dhabi-based IHC’s about $1 billion in Sammaan Capital; and a $11.5 billion joint intent for an integrated aluminium plant in Odisha. Those three alone are a large slice of the “next $25 billion” story. An Invest India office in the UAE is due before end-2026.⁠

Trade is bigger and more solid than the investment headline. India–UAE goods-and-services trade hit about $101.25 billion in FY 2025–26. Non-oil trade was about $76.2 billion in 2025. CEPA (the 2022 trade pact) is four years old; leaders want $200 billion trade by 2032. 

India still imports more from the UAE than it exports (recent year: exports ~$37 billion, imports ~$64 billion). 

Local-currency (rupee–dirham) settlement is growing and is in double digits; one official window cited over 15% of trade invoiced in local currencies from mid-2023 to early 2026. The dirham is dollar-pegged, so this is easier than with a floating Gulf currency.⁠

Where they want the new money: ports and shipbuilding (six workstreams: own ships, build ports, make/repair/break ships, make containers), energy security (oil reserves, LPG/LNG, possible subsea gas pipeline), plus space, logistics, startups, stock market, AI, food and aviation. 

India says port capacity doubled in 10 years and may need to double again; Vadhavan and east- and west-coast ports were named.

Коррупция границ не признаёт: как эстонские коррупционеры переезжают в Латвию

В Эстонии вовсю полыхает скандал вокруг закупок боеприпасов для Украины: заплатили почти 60 миллионов евро, а снаряды оказались непригодными. Министр обороны подал в отставку, делом занимается Европейская прокуратура. 

Казалось бы, при чем здесь Латвия? А при том, что люди, стоявшие в центре этого скандала, уже обосновались там и развивают оборонные проекты.

Первая группа — организаторы: Кусти Салм, Мартин Херем и Вейко-Велло Палм. Салм был канцлером Минобороны Эстонии, Херем — командующим Силами обороны, а сейчас он кандидат на пост министра обороны. Именно Салм, по данным журналистов, создавал систему закупок, которая привела к коррупционному скандалу. 

Теперь все трое работают в Frankenburg Technologies — Салм гендиректор, Херем стратегический советник, Палм член правления. И эта же компания в июне 2026 года открыла в Риге завод по сборке ракет. Инвестиции — более 10 миллионов евро, планы — до 100 ракет в день.

Вторая группа — исполнители: Магнус-Вальдемар Саар и Катри Раудсепа. Саар возглавлял Центр оборонных инвестиций Эстонии (RKIK), Раудсепа была его заместителем, а после ухода Саара временно возглавила центр. Именно они подписывали контракты с фирмой-прокладкой Datasel, которая поставила некачественные снаряды. 

Теперь оба руководят компанией Wolfram Europa и продвигают в Екабпилсе проект завода боеприпасов стоимостью 200 миллионов евро.

Схема очевидна: первые трое создали коррупционную схему в Эстонии, «поработали», ушли в частный бизнес и перенесли активность в Латвию. Вторые — те, кто непосредственно подписывал провальные контракты, — пошли по тому же пути. Они увидели, что в Латвии можно делать дела, и «соскочили» из Эстонии, притащив в Латвию свои коррупционные навыки. 

А что говорят в Риге? А там спокойны: мол, это всего лишь один эпизод в их насыщенной событиями жизни. Ничего страшного, «будем посмотреть».

«Эта информация о том, что происходит в Эстонии, появилась сейчас. Если эта компания продолжает работать и развиваться, это один случай, который с ними произошел. Что будет дальше, что решит суд и что решит их правительство, что компания будет делать — это надо смотреть. Это надо будет учитывать тогда, когда эта компания предложит нам закупить какую-то свою продукцию»,
 — указывает министр обороны Латвии Райвис Мелнис.

А тем временем Wolfram Europa уже претендует на поддержку латвийского государства в программе крупных инвестиций — скидку на капитал до 4,9 миллиона евро. И, судя по настрою их латвийского коллеги Мелниса, всё может получиться.

Передвижной цирк-шапито из Эстонии продолжает прибалтийское турне. Кошельки латвийских налогоплательщиков под угрозой.

Owning a pucca house is a dream for every individual. During his election campaign in Bengal, Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji had mentioned the plight of Jute Mill workers and promised pucca houses for them if BJP government comes in power. To turn that promise into reality, our government, under the leadership of Hon’ble @SuvenduWB ji, has taken an initiative to provide affordable housing for jute mill workers.

At an important announcement was made in a Press Conference at the Labour Department today, it was decided to facilitate affordable housing for eligible EWS-category jute mill workers on a pilot basis in North 24 Parganas and Hooghly districts under the Affordable Housing in Partnership ( #AHP ) component of PMAY-Urban 2.0.

Eligible worker families with an annual household income of up to ₹3 lakh and who do not own a pucca house anywhere in the country will be eligible to benefit from this initiative.

Each housing unit will have a carpet area of 30–45 square metres (approximately 320–485 square feet), with at least two rooms, a kitchen and a toilet. The estimated construction cost of each flat will be approximately ₹5.50 lakh. Of this, ₹1.50 lakh will be contributed by the Central Government, ₹2.79 lakh by the State Government, and ₹50,000 by the beneficiary. The remaining approximately ₹71,000 will be borne by the Labour Welfare Board of the Labour Department.

In North 24 Parganas, Bhatpara, Titagarh and Kamarhati Municipalities have been directed to identify suitable and dispute-free government land for the project. In Hooghly, special camps will be organised with the assistance of the Labour Department and the Labour Commissionerate to help workers submit their applications. Around 8,000 #jute mill #workers have already expressed interest in this initiative.

The Labour Department will coordinate with the district administration, municipalities, workers’ organisations and mill managements to facilitate the identification of eligible beneficiaries and the application process.

The primary objective of this initiative is to improve the quality of life of jute mill workers and their families by providing them with safe, secure and dignified housing.

TCS paid shareholders ₹39,437 crore in the year to March 2026, the most of 1,628 listed companies that paid a dividend, and ₹18,731 crore more than second-placed HDFC Bank.

HOW TO READ IT
A dividend is a share of profit paid in cash to shareholders. Top 10 of 1,628 companies that paid one, year to March 2026.

WHAT STANDS OUT
- TCS leads HDFC Bank by ₹18,731 crore, almost double the second place, even though HDFC Bank's own profit was larger.
- Four of the top 10 are government-owned companies (ONGC, Coal India, SBI, Indian Oil), more than any other kind in the list.
- Three of the top 10 are software companies (TCS, Infosys, HCLTech), the only private-sector group with more than one entry.

HOW IT IS MEASURED
A dividend is cash a company pays out of its profit to the people who own its shares. The figure here is "dividends paid" from the cash part of each company's own yearly accounts (its cash flow statement) for the year to March 2026: the cash that actually left the company as dividends during the year. That includes the final dividend for the year before, which is paid after the yearly shareholders' meeting, so it is not the same as the dividends announced for the year. It is the company's own accounts (standalone), not its group's (consolidated): a group's figure also counts dividends that companies it owns paid to their other shareholders, which is not money paid to the company's own shareholders. Where a year has more than one version on file, the latest is used. 5,331 listed companies filed full-year results for the year; 1,628 show a dividend paid. A zero in these accounts can mean "not reported" as well as "paid nothing", so no count of companies that paid nothing is given. As a check against reading errors, a company is ranked only when its dividends are no more than 3 times its profit for the year and, where it paid one the year before, between 0.2 and 5 times that figure; 1,478 payers are ranked and 150 are set aside (14 over 3 times profit, 34 under 0.2 times last year, 30 over 5 times last year, 72 with no profit figure). None of the companies not ranked could have made the ten on the evidence we hold for them (the same year's group accounts, else 5 times the year before). 3,508 companies show no dividend in any account we hold (this year, their group's, or last year); 2,723 of them made too little profit to reach the ten under the 3-times-profit rule and 759 own less in total than the 10th amount; 6 bigger ones (Reliance Communications, Meesho, Indus Towers, Adani Power, Vodafone Idea, Indian Overseas Bank) show a zero in every account and are not ranked; 20 (Sanofi Cons Healthc Ind, Foseco India, Huhtamaki India, Schaeffler India, Enkei Wheels (India), Crisil, Rain Industries, Dic India, John Cockerill India, Varun Beverages and others) have no figures for the year at all and cannot be checked. Each coin on the poster is ₹1,000 crore and the top coin of each stack is cut to the exact amount. A big dividend total mostly reflects a big company. It says nothing about what one share pays compared with its price, and nothing about whether the company is good, cheap or well run.
