The strategy?

Acquire → Turnaround → Integrate → Expand

⚡ POWER:
The biggest proof of the playbook

Adani Power's acquired portfolio now includes 7.45 GW of thermal capacity, with 7+ GW reportedly turned around.

Some striking examples:

• Raipur: EBITDA ₹210 Cr → ₹2,350 Cr (FY20-FY26)
• Raigarh: -₹100 Cr → ₹1,110 Cr
• Mahan: ₹550 Cr → ₹1,600 Cr (FY22-FY26)

The next step is even more interesting: these acquired plants are becoming platforms for brownfield expansion, using existing land, transmission connections & infrastructure.

Adani Power could increase capacity from 18.3 GW to ~42 GW by FY32, supported by a 23.72 GW expansion programme worth ~₹2 lakh crore.

Around 60% of this planned capacity is brownfield & 56% is tied to long-term PPAs.

⚓ PORTS:

Key acquisitions include:

• Dighi — ₹705 Cr
• Krishnapatnam — ₹13,675 Cr
• Karaikal — ₹1,485 Cr
• Gopalpur — ₹3,080 Cr

At Karaikal alone, another ₹850 Cr is being invested in upgrades, capacity expansion & a new container terminal.

Adani Ports is targeting 1 billion tonnes of annual cargo by 2030, with domestic volumes targeted at 850 MT.

⚡ ENERGY TRANSMISSION:

Adani Energy Solutions acquired transmission assets from Reliance Infrastructure for ₹1,000 Cr & Mumbai's integrated power business for ₹18,800 Cr.

Today, AESL has:

• 14,000+ km transmission network
• 23,000+ MVA transformation capacity
• ₹20,000–25,000 Cr annual capex guidance
• ₹1.1 lakh Cr near-term transmission bidding pipeline
• ₹29,500 Cr smart-meter projects under execution

✈️ AIRPORTS:

Adani acquired Mumbai International Airport from GVK in 2021 for ₹15,000 Cr, eventually building an 8-airport portfolio.

The platform now handles roughly:

• 23% of India's passenger traffic
• 29% of air cargo
• ~96 million passengers in FY26

Navi Mumbai Airport has added an initial 20 million passengers/year of capacity.

AAHL is also raising ₹9,825 Cr (~$1B) from Alpha Wave Global, Premji Invest, Temasek & BlackRock-managed funds at an ~$18B pre-money valuation.

The money will support expansion toward ~200 million annual passenger capacity & ~22 million sq. ft. of first-phase Airport City development.

🌱 RENEWABLES:

Adani Green initially used acquisitions such as Essel Green's solar portfolio to build scale.

The platform added 3.4 GW solar + 0.7 GW wind + 1 GW hybrid capacity in FY26.

Management targets 50 GW by 2030, while battery storage is expected to exceed 10 GWh by FY27.

And now comes the bigger picture.

Adani Enterprises' annual capex has risen from roughly ₹8,500-9,000 Cr in 2022 to ₹30,000-35,000 Cr recently.

Jefferies estimates roughly ₹2 lakh crore of cumulative investment between FY26-FY31 across airports, data centres, new energy, roads, defence, copper & other businesses.

This is essentially Adani's “incubate → scale → demerge” playbook evolving into something bigger:

Buy assets → improve them → connect them to the network → reinvest → create new infrastructure platforms.

The interesting part isn't simply the ₹1 lakh crore spent on acquisitions.

It's what happens after the acquisition.

Global Exchange Comparison
- CME Group: 23.8x P/E.

- NSE: 43.0x P/E.

Growth vs Valuation
- Macquarie sees 65% P/E premium.
- NSE reportedly delivers ~60% higher growth.
- India’s financialisation supports structural growth.
- Macquarie target price: ₹1,965.
- PL Research estimates 11% annual growth.
- ICE expected growth: ~12%.
- Nasdaq expected growth: ~13%.
- Global peers trade near ~25x P/E.

Market Views
- Some investors see positives as priced in.
- Long-term financialisation remains a structural tailwind.
- Regulatory volume impact may be temporary.
- Volumes could normalise over several quarters.
- Dominant market share supports NSE's premium.
- Superior margins also support the valuation.
- Near-term growth expectations remain debated.

KEY TAKEAWAY
NSE commands a significant valuation premium versus global exchanges, trading at 43x FY26 earnings. The premium is supported by its growth, margins, market share and India's financialisation opportunity, while the key debate remains whether future growth justifies the elevated multiple.

Carysil Ltd | Plant Visit & Management Meet Notes

We recently visited Carysil’s manufacturing facility in Bhavnagar, Gujarat, on 25th September 2026, as part of a site visit organised by Go India Advisors (@goindiastocks ).

The visit provided first-hand insights into Carysil’s manufacturing capabilities, capacity constraints, customer relationships, product innovation, India Growth strategy and its transition towards an integrated kitchen & bathroom solutions platform.

Here are some key takeaways: 👇

1. Capacity is increasingly becoming the key constraint

Quartz sinks remain the core business. The plant is operating at high utilisation(88%), with mould availability and carrier capacity emerging as practical bottlenecks. The company currently has 10 lakh annual quartz-sink capacity, with another 2.5 lakh units planned.

Stainless-steel sinks are even tighter: 2.5 lakh annual capacity is operating at ~91.6% utilisation, with another 1.5 lakh units of capacity planned.

2. Manufacturing integration is deepening

What stood out at the plant was the increasing level of in-house capability — from moulds, dies and tooling to press-shop operations, CNC machining, PVD finishing and appliance assembly.

Bringing more processes in-house should provide greater control over cost, lead times, product development and quality, while reducing dependence on external vendors.

3. Quartz has a strong global OEM franchise

The quartz business remains predominantly OEM-led, with the plant indicating roughly 80% OEM / 20% own-brand mix. Global relationships include customers such as IKEA, Home Depot, Lowe’s and other large kitchen retailers/brands.

An interesting opportunity is the combination of OEM scale + proprietary manufacturing capabilities + increasing own-brand presence.

4. India could become an important second growth engine

Management is pushing aggressively into India through brand stores, dealers, e-commerce, B2B and the Karesi brand.

Domestic revenue was ~₹178 Cr in FY26, with management targeting ₹500 Cr by FY29/FY30. The company also plans significant investment in brand stores, including 50–60 stores, while Karesi is being positioned to address the mid-segment without diluting Carysil’s premium positioning.

5. Product portfolio is expanding beyond sinks

Faucets, kitchen appliances, RO/water solutions and integrated kitchen offerings are being developed as the next growth vectors.

The stainless-steel faucet opportunity is particularly interesting as the company positions the products as lead-free, with manufacturing capabilities including CNC machining, drilling and PVD finishing.

6. Technology remains a key differentiator

The plant showcased multiple manufacturing routes across deep-drawn stainless-steel sinks, handmade sinks and PVD finishes, while the quartz business is built around formulation, mould-making, casting and finishing capabilities.

Management is also preparing to launch premium nano-technology products, aimed at improving product performance and differentiation.

7. The biggest near-term watchpoint is execution: Management is maintaining 15% CAGR guidance, while current challenges include container availability, freight and elevated input costs. Current expansion is expected to add 2.5 lakh sink capacity, followed by another ~₹300 Cr of CapEx over 5 years aimed at supporting ~₹1,000 Cr of incremental revenue.

Our key takeaway: The plant visit made the strategic transition visible on the ground — from a global sink/OEM manufacturer towards a vertically integrated, multi-category kitchen & bathroom solutions platform.

Capacity + technology + India brand-building + new categories will be the key variables to watch from here.

At 43 Times Earnings, NSE Valued Way Higher Than Global Peers

NSE's Debut and Valuation
National Stock Exchange of India (NSE) made its debut on the BSE last week and ranks among the top dozen firms in terms of market capitalisation

At ₹1,792 per share, it is valued at ₹4.44 trillion, ahead of Titan, Infosys and Kotak Mahindra Bank and nearly three-and-a-half times of BSE

At 43 times FY26 earnings, it is only next to Titan (73x) and Adani Enterprises (100x), but cheaper than its smaller peer BSE

NSE made a lacklustre debut at ₹1,800 per share against its issue price of ₹1,785 apiece on Thursday

Just days before, the stock had been trading near the ₹2000 mark in unlisted markets

Now, it is the seventh-largest exchange in the world by market capitalisation, which stood at $4.4 trillion on Friday's close

Brokerage Views
Macquarie said in a report last week that while NSE trades at a 65% P/E premium to international exchanges, it delivers about 60% higher growth and returns, supported by India's structural financialisation tailwinds

It has a 12-month target of ₹1,965 for the stock, implying 9.6% upside from Friday's close at ₹1,792.65

Based on a PL research report, NSE is expected to grow at 11% annually for the next three years. At 43 times earnings the valuation appears to be expensive

On the other hand, ICE (NYSE) is expected to grow at 12% and Nasdaq at 13% for the same period but trade at a P/E multiple of around 25 times

Vikas Gupta, CEO at OmniScience Capital, said he does not see regulatory actions as a major risk to NSE's volumes. Any impact on volumes following regulatory actions, he said, may be transitory, with volumes likely to normalise over a few quarters as India's financial-market penetration continues to rise

Elios Financial Services' Sham Chandak, head of institutional equities, said that NSE at current market cap is at a significant premium to other global exchanges because of its superior margins, demonstrated high growth for a long period of time, and dominant market share

Every market recap is framing IRDAI's consultation paper as bad news for insurance distributors. I read it as the regulator finally doing something about a broken sales machine.

India's insurance penetration is 3.7% of GDP, less than half the global average of 7.3%. Yet IRDAI logged 26,600 mis-selling complaints in FY25 alone, up 14% from the year before. You do not fix low penetration by letting banks shove unsuitable policies down borrowers' throats to earn a fat commission.

The trigger for this is clear. IRDAI scrapped product-wise commission caps in 2023 for a broader expense ceiling. Insurers responded by competing aggressively for distributors, and some breached the limits. So now the regulator wants to pull the EoM ceiling down gradually over five years and simplify the whole distribution network into three categories.

Policybazaar and Turtlemint have fallen 30% since the news. I get why. Commission income is their business model, and less generosity from insurers means thinner margins.

But here is where I might be wrong. Cheaper distribution sounds great until you remember that good advice costs money. If commissions shrink too far, the pushy bank agent survives and the helpful advisor stops being viable. I am not sure IRDAI has cracked that part yet, and it worries me more than any stock price.

My bank tried to bundle insurance with a home loan once. I said no and got the loan anyway. If these rules pass, the next borrower might not need my stubbornness. Are you seeing this trend where you bank, or still getting the hard sell?

My End of Q1FY27 Analysis Summary Part 3

​Continuing the watchlist dive. This time focusing on businesses capturing structural shifts in data centers, electronics manufacturing, platform businesses & clean energy.

​1] Data Center Infra

​1)Netweb Technologies: 

Doing end-to-end data center and cloud infrastructure setups. A less asset-heavy model. 62% of revenue is now coming from the AI segment, sitting on a ₹500 Cr order book. High repetition rate from clients (98%) and guiding for 30-40% growth.

​2)E2E Networks: 

An asset-heavy model where they build data centers (buying expensive NVIDIA GPUs) and rent out cloud computing capacity. Monthly recurring revenue is doubling YoY. Backed by a 21% stake from L&T.

​3)Aeroflex Industries: 

Shifting focus from traditional metal hoses for oil/gas to liquid cooling systems for AI data centers. Cooling skids are priced around ₹2.5-3 lakh each, and they are aggressively expanding capacity from 9,000 to 15,000 skids by Q3 FY27.

​2] Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS)

2.1)​Syrma SGS: 

Guiding for 35% growth. FY28 looks even stronger as their new PCB assembly facility comes online. Shifting focus away from low-margin box builds toward high-margin ODM models.

2.2)​Amtron Electronics (SME):

Operating in high-margin segments (medical, EV tech, AI, aerospace) yielding an industry-leading 22-23% EBITDA margin.

​3] Electronics Retailing

​3.1)Aditya Vision (AVL):

Dominating the Hindi heartland (Bihar, UP, Jharkhand) and now expanding into Chhattisgarh, MP, and West Bengal. Consistent 25-30 store additions yearly with strong 10-11% margins.

3.2)​Electronics Mart India (EMI): 

A turnaround story. The initial drag from their North India (Delhi/NCR) expansion is breaking even, boosting consolidated margins.

​3.3)GNG Electronics:

Capitalizing on the supply-demand gap in the refurbished/used laptop market. Average selling prices are moving up from ₹25k to over ₹30k, expanding PAT margins.

​4] Platform Businesses

4.1)​CarTrade Tech: 

A brilliant asset-light platform model. The OLX acquisition is turning into a game-changer for them, driving high-margin subscriptions via the Elite Buyer program (adding 5,000+ daily). Management is guiding for ₹1,000 Cr PAT by FY30.
​Paytm: UPI MDR charge structures and cross-selling (loans, broking, MTF) are providing tailwinds. Management aiming to push EBITDA margins from 8% to the 15-20% range.

4.2)Eternal (​Zomato & Blinkit):

Blinkit has hit EBITDA breakeven and is narrowing losses rapidly.They are growing via margin preservation rather than heavy discounting, making them the clear leader in quick commerce.

​4.3)Nykaa: 

Beauty (70% of revenue) continues to thrive as international brands prefer listing on their platform rather than spending massive CAPEX on physical retail.

​4.4)urum PropTech:

Transitioning from loss-making to reporting positive PAT over the last three quarters. The https://t.co/GodTKOJTdV acquisition consolidates the real estate discovery ecosystem.

​5] Clean Energy

​5.1)Acme Solar: 

Shifting into Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to capture peak evening electricity prices (₹8-10 vs ₹4-5 daytime). Expanding BESS capacity from 3-4 GW to 10 GW by FY27 & 25 GW by FY30.

​5.2)CleanMax: 

Capturing industrial & AI data center demand, with AI contributing 40-45% of revenues. (Monitorable: grid curtailment issues in Rajasthan).

​6] Defense & Aerospace

6.1)​MTAR : 

Diversified across clean energy (Fuel cells for Bloom Energy make up 60% of revenue), nuclear reactors, and now data centers. Guiding for 80% revenue growth at 24% margins.

​6.2)IdeaForge: 

A pure play on the structural shift toward drone warfare. Order book is massive, but execution pace and margin pressure are the key monitorables.

​6.3)Apollo Micro Systems:

Getting into underwater & land mines alongside aerospace components. 40-50% growth guidance, though execution remains a tracking point.

Business Segments

आज कंपनी का मुख्य business engine Indian Railways के लिए 25+ RDSO-certified safety spares का manufacturing है। इसके साथ कंपनी एक दूसरे business engine का निर्माण कर रही है, जिसके माध्यम से आगे चलकर इसी manufacturing capability को complete bogies और wagons तक विस्तार देने की योजना है।

1. Critical Safety Spares — वे components जिनके बिना train workshop से बाहर नहीं निकल सकती

कंपनी द्वारा बेचा जाने वाला प्रत्येक component RDSO certification की regulatory requirement से गुजरता है। यह certification एक महत्वपूर्ण entry barrier बनाता है, क्योंकि केवल approved vendors ही इन safety-critical railway components की supply कर सकते हैं।

RDSO Certification — मुख्य entry barrier

RDSO यानी Research Designs & Standards Organisation, Indian Railways की प्रमुख standards organisation है।

कंपनी के पास Class ‘A’ certification है, जिसे highest foundry grade के रूप में प्रस्तुत किया गया है। इसके अलावा कंपनी के पास:

ISO 9001 — Quality Management
ISO 14001 — Environmental Management
ISO 45001 — Occupational Health & Safety

जैसे certifications भी हैं।

महत्वपूर्ण बात यह है कि RDSO approval केवल एक बार मिलने वाली औपचारिकता नहीं है। नए competitors को भी इसी approval process को पूरा करना पड़ता है, जिसके कारण safety-critical railway component segment में entry आसान नहीं है।

उत्तराखंड में स्थित लगभग 10,000 sq. metre का manufacturing plant कई महत्वपूर्ण manufacturing processes को एक ही location पर integrate करता है।

इससे quality control और lead-time management पर कंपनी का direct control बढ़ता है।

Ramkrishna Forgings Ltd :  Where is the growth coming from ?

Management has stated a target of Rs 10,000 Cr revenue by FY30, with an expectation of around 15–20% annual volume growth.

The interesting part is how they plan to get there.

The growth story is not just about the existing auto business:

• Railways JV  : a key growth opportunity, including higher-value products
• Non-auto segments : increasing diversification beyond traditional CV forgings
• Exports : expanding the international customer base
• Capacity additions :  creating room for future volume growth
• New products : moving towards more complex and higher-value components

So the broader story is about moving up the value chain while diversifying the business.

Rs 10,000 Cr by FY30 is the ambition. 
Now the interesting part is to track the numbers quarter after quarter and see whether the revenue growth, margins and new businesses start reflecting that ambition.

The next few quarters should tell us a lot.

Shriram Pistons / SPR Auto - The Antolin acquisition added interiors and lighting—and management indicates that the acquired businesses’ EBITDA margin has improved from roughly 7–8% before acquisition to the early/mid-teens.

But scale is still being taxed by integration friction and acquisition funding. Q1 carried about ₹25.2 Cr of additional finance cost, while net debt was approximately ₹550 Cr in June 2026.

So the thesis is no longer “a larger piston maker.” It is whether SPR can turn acquired revenue into platform economics:
• preserve Antolin’s margin gains
• repay acquisition debt with operating cash
• increase non-engine content through interiors, lighting and EV motors/controllers

Even the rename to SPR Auto Technologies is a strategic move. The company wants to be valued on a wider automotive-technology perimeter—not only its legacy powertrain franchise.

The next proof is simple: consolidated margins should hold while finance cost and net debt fall. If revenue scales but PAT conversion remains weak, the platform thesis is premature.

Why Chennai Is Losing the Data Centre Race to Hyderabad

The Core Shift
Hyderabad could overtake Chennai as India's second-largest data centre market within the next four years, as land and power constraints limit Chennai's ability to add new capacity

Hyderabad expected to add 695MW, or exactly twice the 347MW data centre capacity Chennai is projected to add over the next four years

Said an 8 September report by real estate consulting firm Cushman & Wakefield

Why the Shift
Stakeholders Mint spoke to and reports reviewed point to a widening infrastructure advantage for Hyderabad

Availability of land, power and large-scale campuses draws data centre investments away from more constrained locations such as Chennai

Ambattur (in north-west Chennai) and Siruseri (to the south) have developed strong ecosystems, but further concentration increases pressure on land and utilities

Shortage of large land parcels there, and the absence of a third area where data centres can be built, are significant constraints — particularly for hyperscale projects requiring hundreds of acres and long-term power visibility, said Ravi Agrawal (attributed name from article), noting that constraint is helping newer locations attract the next wave of large data centre projects

The Bigger Picture — Sector Expansion
India's data centre industry is entering a rapid expansion phase, with operational capacity expected to more than triple from 1,789 MW in June 2026 to about 5.65GW by the end of 2030

Implies annualised growth of 33%, according to Cushman & Wakefield

Meeting this demand will require significant capital, with JLL estimating the sector needs about $110 billion in investments by 2029

By December 2030, Hyderabad is expected to account for 15%, or 838MW, of India's operational data centre capacity

Chennai, with a projected 562MW, will account for 10% of the country's 5.65GW of capacity

Mumbai, by far, will remain India's largest data centre market, with an expected 2.63GW of capacity

Analyst Take — Vijay Agrawal (Equirus Capital)
Managing director of infrastructure at Equirus Capital: key challenge for Chennai, which today has above 50% more operational data centre capacity than Hyderabad, is the concentration of data centre clusters, which is straining land availability and infrastructure development

Recent Moves in Hyderabad & Visakhapatnam
In Hyderabad, Microsoft's latest data centre was operationalized on 21 September, while Tata Consultancy Services has planned a 1GW data centre

In Visakhapatnam, Google is constructing a 1GW data centre in partnership with Adani Enterprises, while Meta Platforms, in partnership with Sify Technologies, has announced a 500MW data centre plan

Advantage for these regions is the availability of land and state governments' willingness to facilitate data centre investments

SECTION 12 — EV & AUTOMOTIVE PRECISION ENGINEERING

EVs are not eliminating precision engineering.
They are changing WHERE the precision is required.

1. WHAT CHANGES WITH EVs?
Traditional ICE engine components such as:
Pistons
Valves
Crankshafts

Become less dominant.

At the same time, demand increases for:

E-axle gears
Motor shafts
Rotor laminations
Precision transmission components

GEARS DO NOT DISAPPEAR.

EV gear systems can operate at much higher rotational speeds.

That creates greater requirements for:

Gear accuracy
Surface finish
Noise
Vibration
Harshness (NVH)
Balancing

Grinding becomes increasingly important rather than relying only on conventional hobbing.

2. THERMAL MANAGEMENT

This is one of the major new precision-engineering areas in EVs.

Components include:

Chillers
Coolant valves
Heat-exchanger plates
Cooling channels
Thermal-management assemblies

These require precision:

Brazing
Stamping
Machining
Leak testing
Surface finishing

The EV is essentially creating a much larger thermal-management ecosystem.

3. BATTERY MANUFACTURING EQUIPMENT

Battery manufacturing itself creates another precision-engineering opportunity.

Equipment includes:

Precision rolls
Slitters
Coating dies
Formation equipment
Cell-production machinery

This is a completely new machine ecosystem compared with traditional ICE manufacturing.

The source notes that Indian cell-equipment manufacturing is still embryonic and much of the equipment is currently imported, particularly from China and Korea.

 As an Importer/Trader: Through its Integrated Resources Management (IRM) division, Adani is India’s largest private coal trader.  As a Supplier in Government Tenders: When state utilities or public sector power producers like NTPC float tenders to import coal for blending, Adani Enterprises routinely bids for and wins contracts to source and deliver those imported shipments.

Shanti Gold: My Take

I personally do not like the company as I see many reasons to feel uncomfortable. Market was very happy with the Shanti Gold rally and I stayed away even when prices were making new highs. So let’s talk about the reasons why I stayed away even though I love the sector:

1. Promoters:
They have 2 listed companies — Shanti Gold & Utssav CZ. Pankaj Kumar Jagawat is the main promoter in both the companies. No issue in this also, but where I felt some problem was that despite separate managements, promoter was facing investors on behalf of both the companies. So I did not have complete clarity on who is actually running the show and where the main focus of the promoter is.

2. Bottom-line:
Shanti Gold came for IPO and raised funds and bought gold around the time of the gold rally. They made huge returns on unhedged inventory, which was more like a one-off benefit.

For FY27, the targets which they gave indicate that topline can grow around 60–70% or even higher, but profitability may remain almost the same because they already had huge inventory gains sitting in the base.
So even if revenues grow strongly, EPS may remain almost flat because the previous year profitability had support from inventory gains.

3. Promoter Buying:
The promoter was buying shares in Utssav during March–April’26 but did not put similar money in Shanti Gold where his stake is shared with other promoters.

So that was also a factor for me to worry whether the promoter would focus more on the company where he has relatively higher ownership/economic interest rather than the company where the stake is shared with other promoters.

Maybe there is nothing wrong here, but for me it reduced the conviction.

4. Investments in Other Companies:
They have investments in Golkunda Diamonds (competitor), Lalithaa Jewellery (client) and recently after the rights issue they invested again in Ratnaveer Precision.

Again, no issue at all if the company has excessive funds or if they are shifting towards an asset-light model like Sky Gold did.

But they still have to maintain inventories on their books to sell and book revenues. So working capital remains a constraint, especially when they are aggressively expanding and capacities have already more than doubled this year.

Despite ramping up capacities and requiring more working capital, they are also investing money in stock markets.
If I need exposure in other companies, I can invest in them directly.

For me, management should focus more on the core business, capacity utilisation, inventory management and working capital rather than investing too much in other listed companies.

So these were some of the pointers which made me uncomfortable and because of that I did not build any position out of FOMO despite the company trading at relatively low valuations compared to peers.

Sometimes it’s okay to miss some companies where you do not have conviction.

It is better to build positions where you have conviction and where you would be comfortable holding the business for the long term.

Stage 3: Casting / Forging / Extrusion / Powder Metallurgy (near-net-shape blank)
What happens: Metal is shaped close to the final component geometry, minimising machining waste.
Forging: compressive force refines grain flow → stronger parts (crankshafts, turbine discs, landing gear).

Casting: molten metal poured into moulds (complex shapes: pump bodies, turbine blades via investment casting).

Extrusion: metal pushed through dies (aluminium profiles, sections).

Powder metallurgy (PM/MIM): metal powder compacted and sintered — near-net-shape with minimal waste (gears, medical components). MIM (Metal Injection Moulding) makes tiny complex parts (phone hinges, surgical tools).

Machines: Forging presses (up to 10,000+ tonnes), screw presses, hammers; die casting machines (cold/hot chamber); investment casting foundries; extrusion presses; HIP furnaces.

Skills: Die design, metallurgy, process control, NDT certification.

Standards: AMS specs, ASTM, EN; NADCAP for aerospace special processes; PPAP for automotive.
India players: Bharat Forge, Ramkrishna Forgings, MM Forgings, Sundaram Clayton (brake castings + Halol plant), CIE Automotive (Mahindra CIE), Shanthi Gears (gears), Ratnamani Metals (pipes/tubes), Ratnaveer Precision (MIM), INDO-MIM (MIM world leader), Arrow Greentech? no — better: AIA Engineering (castings for mining), Kirloskar Ferrous, Electrosteel (cast iron), Jindal (castings), Hinduja Foundries, Nelcast, Chamber of precision castings: BEPL? Actually precision investment casters: Aequs (Belagavi aerospace cluster), FF aerospace (subsidiaries of US firms), JayJalaram Technologies (listed, investment castings).
Global: Howmet (investment castings — the world leader), Precision Castparts (PCC), thyssenkrupp, AFK (Aichi Steel), Ryobi, Ahresty (die casting), GKN, Arconic.
Value addition: 2–5× on material. Aerospace forgings command the highest premiums.

Entry barriers: Enormous capex, die/tooling know-how, customer qualification cycles of 2–5 years, NADCAP/AS9100 certification.

India competitiveness: Bharat Forge is globally competitive in commercial vehicle and has entered aerospace/defence; India is strong in open-die and automotive forgings; weak in large aerospace closed-die forgings, superalloy disc forgings, single-crystal blade casting (Howmet/PCC territory). This is a genuine national gap.

⚡ Quality Power Electrical Equipments (QPOWER) — Moat & Competitive Edge
Quality Power is an interesting “picks-and-shovels” play on grid modernisation, HVDC, renewable integration and power quality. Its moat is not simply manufacturing capacity; it is the combination of specialised technology + qualification barriers + global customer relationships + engineering know-how.

1. 🔥 The biggest moat: specialised high-voltage equipment
Quality Power operates in areas such as:
HVDC
FACTS
reactors
high-voltage instrument transformers
GIS-related equipment
STATCOM/power electronics
battery-storage power converters
These aren't ordinary electrical components.
They sit inside infrastructure where reliability is far more important than simply getting the cheapest component.
For example, a failure in a high-voltage transmission system can cause enormous economic and operational consequences.
That creates a natural barrier:
Customer doesn't want to experiment with an unproven supplier.

2. 🧪 Qualification moat
This is probably the most underappreciated part of the QPOWER story.
For critical HV equipment, customers generally need:
Design capability → testing → certifications → customer qualification → successful installations → track record
Therefore, a competitor cannot simply say:
"I will manufacture the same product at 10% lower cost."
It needs to establish technical credibility and field history.
This creates a much stronger moat than ordinary manufacturing.

3. 🌍 Global OEM + utility relationships
Quality Power has built relationships across global markets and supplies equipment into demanding applications.
Its management has highlighted customers spanning utilities, renewable developers, data centres and industrial networks, while its technology portfolio is increasingly aimed at global grid-modernisation projects. 
The interesting part is that QPOWER is becoming a technology supplier to the ecosystem, rather than merely a contract manufacturer.
That distinction matters.

4. ⚡ HVDC is a particularly attractive niche
Think of HVDC simply as:
Electricity needs to travel very long distances → AC becomes inefficient in certain applications → HVDC becomes attractive.
India's renewable resources are often far away from consumption centres.
For example:
Rajasthan solar/wind → transmission network → Mumbai/Delhi/industrial centres
This requires substantial transmission infrastructure.
Quality Power supplies specialised equipment used in this ecosystem.
And globally, offshore wind + renewable integration + cross-border transmission are increasing the need for HVDC.
The company's FY25 presentation specifically identified HVDC and FACTS projects as important growth drivers. 

5. 🔌 FACTS gives another layer of differentiation
FACTS = Flexible AC Transmission Systems.
In simple terms:
FACTS equipment helps the grid control voltage, power flow and stability.
As renewable penetration rises, grids become more complicated.
Solar/wind are variable.
Therefore the grid increasingly needs:
generation + transmission + voltage control + power-quality management + storage
Quality Power participates in several of these layers.
That gives it exposure to the complexity of the energy transition, not just the volume of electricity generation.

6. 🏭 Mehru acquisition strengthened the moat
The acquisition of Mehru Electrical & Mechanical Engineers significantly expanded QPOWER's high-voltage instrument-transformer capabilities.
This is important because QPOWER is building a portfolio of complementary HV technologies rather than relying on one product.

7. 🔄 Vertical integration is quietly becoming important
Quality Power is investing in backward integration, including manufacturing of electrical magnet wire, which management has said is important for its HVDC/FACTS value chain.
It provides:
raw-material security → shorter lead times → better quality control → improved execution → potentially better mrgns

New video: Ramkrishna Forgings — a company still carrying an unresolved FY25 audit red flag just had its promoters put up close to ₹400 Cr of their own cash, at a premium to market, not once but twice. That contradiction is the spine of this one.

Start with the business, because it's genuinely recovering: Q1 FY27 revenue +19.8% YoY, EBITDA +47% YoY, margin expanding to 17.96% for the second straight quarter, PAT nearly tripling. Three optionality legs sit almost entirely outside these numbers — the Ramkrishna-Titagarh Rail Wheel JV (a confirmed ~110,000-wheel utilisation base building toward bulk commercial supply), a new Mexico plant that's just started ramping, and an aerospace/non-ferrous forgings vertical that management says has zero order book today.

Then the governance update, which is what pulled me back into this name this week: promoters committed ₹204.75 Cr via warrants after FY25's inventory discrepancy and qualified audit opinion — that much was known. Turns out it was only half the story. A second, previously undisclosed ₹199.92 Cr warrant program to promoter Chaitanya Jalan has also fully converted, with the final tranche landing just days ago. Combined, that's ~₹404.67 Cr of promoter cash into the company at above-market pricing — roughly double what most coverage, including ours, had captured. Separately, a promoter-group entity holding 3.57% of the company got reclassified out of the promoter group entirely — worth watching, not a red flag on its own.

Here's the part I keep coming back to: capital delivery and audit resolution are two different facts. Promoters following through twice, at a premium, into a company they could have let ride just as easily, is a real signal. My End of Q1FY27 Analysis Summary [Part 2]

​Continuing my sector-wise watchlist tracking. 

Focusing on businesses with high growth, margin expansion, and strong commentary.

​1] Auto & EV Space

1.1)​Ather Energy: 

Moving fast from loss to profit. Their new mass-market scooter expands the customer base beyond premium buyers. Capacity is doubling by Q3 due to strong demand, and their software subscription attach rate is a massive 93%.

​1.2)Mahindra & Mahindra: 

The clear winner in the 4-wheeler SUV trend. Consumer preference is fully shifted to SUVs and M&M is capturing it perfectly

1.3)​Ola Electric: 

On my wait-and-watch list. Need to track how their new dealership model and in-house battery cell manufacturing perform before taking a view.

​2] Dairy Sector 

2.1)​Milky Mist: 

A pure value-added product (VAP) player. They don't sell low-margin raw milk, so they avoid seasonal dips. Focused entirely on high-margin paneer, cheese, and high-protein foods, easily growing at 30-40% through deep distribution.

​3] Hotels & Hospitality

3.1)​Leela Palaces: 

Operating entirely in the ultra-luxury segment. Despite global travel issues, their domestic business grew 25-30% in Q1 without them having to drop room rates to fill beds. Planning aggressive expansion from 4,000 to 10,000 rooms by FY30.

​4] Logistics

​4.1)Shadowfax: 

Taking market share in the fast-growing express delivery space. They recently turned profitable and confidently upgraded their growth guidance from 30% to 40%.
The only monitorable is their high dependence on Meesho.

4.2)​Shiprocket: 

Asset-light platform model. The core shipping business is doing well, and new segments like warehousing are driving revenue, though still at a loss. Note that Q3 is usually weak for them as D2C brands shift to Flipkart/Amazon for festive sales.

​5] Alcohol Beverages 

5.1)​Piccadily Agro: 

A pure premiumization story. Their 'Indri' single malt is a massive hit. They are spinning off their low-margin sugar business next year to become a pure luxury alcohol play, guiding for 60% to 70% growth.

5.2)​Radico Khaitan: 

Steadily moving away from mass-market liquor into high-margin premium brands (like Rampur), which is naturally expanding their operating margins.

​6] Pharma (Oncology & CDMO)

6.1)​Sakar Healthcare:

Heavily focused on the fast-growing Oncology space, aiming to take it from 30% to 70% of total revenue. Partnered with Intas for European distribution and guiding for 35% top-line growth.

​6.2)Shilpa Medicare:

Getting strong approvals in highly regulated markets for high-margin biosimilars.

6.3)​OneSource: 

Massively expanding capacity (from 20,000 to 1.5 lakh) to manufacture high-demand GLP-1 weight loss injections for export markets.

6.4)​Kwality Pharma:

 Another strong Oncology player that just upgraded its revenue guidance to ₹700 Cr.

Pharma Sector needs vigorous tracking just like every other Sector!

النموذج القوي لا يعني بالضرورة إن عندك حل Agentic فعّال.
في الـ Agentic AI، السؤال مش مين عنده أقوى Model. السؤال: مين بنى أفضل System للـ job المطلوب؟
وفي البزنس، الذكاء وحده مش المنتج.
الأداء في السياق هو المنتج.

، والـ Routing يحدد مين يستخدم إمتى. الهدف هنا مش استعراض قوة الـ Model، الهدف إن النظام ككل يحقق أفضل نتيجة ممكنة بشكل موثوق وفعال. وطبعاً أسئلة زي مكان الاستضافة، أمن البيانات، والامتثال مهمة جداً، خصوصاً في بيئات الـ Enterprise. لكن دي كلها أجزاء من الصورة.

لأن الحل الجيد ممكن يعتمد على أكثر من Model أو Capability حسب المهمة، مستوى التعقيد، متطلبات الأمان، التكلفة، وسرعة التنفيذ.مثلاً، مش كل خطوة محتاجة أقوى Model متاح. بعض المهام ممكن تتعامل معها Models أبسط، بينما الحالات الأكثر تعقيداً تروح لـ Model أقوى

في التفكير الأول، السؤال بيكون: مين أذكى؟ مين أقوى؟ مين عنده benchmark أعلى؟
لكن في التفكير الثاني، السؤال بيتغير: مين يشتغل أفضل داخل الـ workflow؟ مين يتكامل مع الأنظمة الموجودة؟ مين يعرف حدود القرار؟ مين يتعامل مع الاستثناءات؟ ومين يحقق النتيجة المطلوبة بتكلفة مناسبة؟

لأنك في النهاية مش بتشتري Model واحد، أنت بتشتري حل كامل تم تصميمه عشان يشتغل داخل بيئة عمل حقيقية.
وده هو الفرق بين التفكير في Single Model والتفكير في Compound AI System.

أحياناً بعض العملاء بيسألوا سؤال بسيط جداً: إيه الـ Model اللي بتستخدموه؟ وهل هو فعلاً بنفس قوة الـ leading models الموجودة اليوم؟ والسؤال منطقي، خصوصاً مع كل الكلام عن أقوى Model، أذكى Model، وأحدث Model.
لكن بالنسبة لي، دي مش الطريقة الصحيحة لتقييم حل Agentic AI.

सोचिए एक ही झटके में किसी कंपनी के शेयर 36% तक ज़मीन पर आ गिरें! बड़े-बड़े बैंक, दिग्गज इंश्योरेंस कंपनियाँ और करोड़ों की फंडिंग वाले फिनटेक जायंट्स सन्नाटे में आ जाएं... आखिर ऐसा क्या ला दिया देश के बीमा रेगुलेटर IRDAI ने?"

"क्या यह आपकी जेब के लिए खुशखबरी है? या फिर लाखों एजेंटों और बैंकों की कमाई का 'गेम ओवर'?
चलिए विस्तार से समझते है …'इन्श्योरेंस का नया नियम: राहत या आफत?'"

भारतीय बीमा विनियामक और विकास प्राधिकरण (IRDAI) ने सितंबर 2026 में बीमा वितरण, कमीशन और बिक्री के तरीकों में भारी सुधार के लिए एक ड्राफ्ट जारी किया है। इसी प्रस्ताव को लेकर देश के बीमा और वित्तीय बाजार में बड़ा बवाल और हलचल मची हुई है।

इस प्रस्ताव का सबसे सीधा असर बीमा बेचने वाले बैंकों, ऑनलाइन एग्रीगेटर प्लेटफॉर्म्स (जैसे PolicyBazaar), NBFCs और एजेंट्स की कमाई पर पड़ने की आशंका है।

शेयर बाजार में गिरावट
IRDAI का यह ड्राफ्ट सामने आते ही शेयर बाजार में इंश्योरेंस और फिनटेक कंपनियों के शेयरों में भारी गिरावट देखने को मिली…

 PolicyBazaar (PB Fintech) के शेयर एक ही दिन में रिकॉर्ड 36% तक गिर गए।
 Max Life, HDFC Life, ICICI Prudential और SBI जैसी प्रमुख बीमा कंपनियों व बैंकों के शेयरों पर भी बुरा असर पड़ा।
 
ब्रोकरेज फर्म्स और विश्लेषकों का मानना है कि यदि यह प्रस्ताव लागू होता है, तो इंश्योरेंस डिस्ट्रीब्यूटर्स और बैंकों की कमीशन से होने वाली आय घट जाएगी।

दरअसल IRDAI ने पॉलिसीधारकों के हितों की रक्षा और गलत तरीके से पॉलिसी बेचने (Mis-selling) को रोकने के लिए कई सख्त प्रस्ताव रखे हैं…

कमीशन पर दोबारा कैप (सीमा) लगाना:
 वर्ष 2023 में IRDAI ने कमीशन की सीमा हटा दी थी, जिसे अब दोबारा लागू करने का प्रस्ताव है।

 पहले वर्ष में मिलने वाले भारी-भरकम कमीशन (जो कई मामलों में 40% या उससे अधिक होता था) को घटाकर उत्पादों के हिसाब से 5% से 20-25% के दायरे में लाने का सुझाव है।

एजेंट/एजेंसी को बड़ा एकमुश्त कमीशन देने के बजाय कमीशन को पॉलिसी की पूरी अवधि (Tenure) में बांटकर देने की बात कही गई है।
￼￼
बैंकाश्योरेंस (बैंकों द्वारा बीमा बिक्री) और लोन-लिंक्ड बीमा पर सख्ती:
बैंक अक्सर ग्राहकों को लोन देते समय जबरन बीमा पॉलिसी खरीदने के लिए दबाव बनाते थे। 

IRDAI ने इस पर रोक लगाने और ग्राहक को किसी भी कंपनी से पॉलिसी चुनने की आजादी देने का प्रस्ताव दिया है।

मल्टी-ब्रांड बेचने वाले बैंकों और कॉर्पोरेट ब्रोकरों के लिए कमीशन की दरें और कम रखी गई हैं।

मोटर इंश्योरेंस (गाड़ियों के बीमा) में बदलाव:
नए वाहनों के अनिवार्य 'थर्ड-पार्टी मोटर बीमा' पर कॉर्पोरेट डिस्ट्रीब्यूटर्स को 0% कमीशन और एजेंट्स को केवल 2.5% देने का प्रस्ताव है।

डिजिटल 'डार्क पैटर्न्स' पर प्रतिबंध:
ऑनलाइन ऐप्स/वेबसाइट्स पर ग्राहकों से बुनियादी जानकारी दिखाने से पहले उनकी निजी डिटेल (फ़ोन नंबर/ईमेल) मांगने पर रोक लगाने का सुझाव है।

बीमा का मूल्य और नियम पारदर्शी रूप से बिना नंबर मांगे दिखाए जाने चाहिए।

मिस-सेलिंग की जवाबदेही (Policy Tagging):
हर बेची गई पॉलिसी को बेचने वाले एजेंट या प्रतिनिधि से डिजिटल रूप से 'टैग' किया जाएगा, ताकि मिस-सेलिंग होने पर जवाबदेही तय की जा सके।

IRDAI ने यह कदम क्यों उठाया?
लागत में भारी बढ़ोतरी: IRDAI के आंकड़ों के अनुसार, वित्तीय वर्ष 2024-25 में बीमा कंपनियों ने ₹60,800 करोड़ कमीशन के रूप में बांटे (18% की वृद्धि), जबकि बीमा प्रीमियम में बढ़ोतरी सिर्फ 6.73% ही हुई।

उपभोक्ताओं को लाभ: कमीशन और वितरण लागत कम होने से बीमा पॉलिसियां सस्ती होंगी और प्रीमियम की दरें घट सकती हैं।

आम जनता पर इसका क्या असर होगा?
आम उपभोक्ताओं के लिए यह प्रस्ताव बेहद फायदेमंद साबित हो सकता है। मिस-सेलिंग रुकेगी, पॉलिसी की दरें (प्रीमियम) सस्ती होंगी और बैंक लोन लेते समय जबरन बीमा नहीं थोप सकेंगे।
 
 नुकसान (एजेंट्स/एजेंसियों के लिए): बीमा एजेंटों, डिजिटल प्लेटफॉर्म्स और बैंकों की फीस/कमीशन से होने वाली कमाई पर सीधी चोट पहुंचेगी।

वर्तमान स्थिति: यह अभी एक ड्राफ्ट (प्रस्ताव) है, जिस पर IRDAI ने सभी पक्षों (कंपनियों, एजेंट्स और जनता) से सुझाव मांगे हैं। अंतिम नियम लागू होने से पहले इनमें कुछ बदलाव या संशोधन की संभावना बनी हुई है।

IRDAI just released a consultation paper on insurance distribution costs, and some of the numbers are wild. Broker commissions grew 2x faster than premium. NBFCs are getting 40%+ payouts. Group health commissions as high as 93%. Distributors are getting paid a lot more, customers are getting a lot less. What it means for brokers, insurers and you 👇 

IRDAI's new consultation paper on distribution costs is worth reading if you track brokers.

FY23 to FY25, premium routed through brokers grew 1.37x. Broker commission grew 2.73x.

Motor: premium +34%, commission +259%

Retail health: avg commission went from ~10% to ~30%
PoSP-led brokers (the Turtlemint type model): avg commission from low single digits to 25-38% in 2 years
Now Policybazaar.

FY26 premium ₹29,934 cr, up 42%
Broking revenue ₹6,089 cr, up 42%
PAT ₹670 cr, up 115%
So roughly 20 paise of revenue for every rupee of premium.

To be fair, PB's revenue is growing in line with premium, not at 2x like the industry. But its book is heavily health (new health +68%), which is the segment IRDAI seems most worried about. And its ₹1,126 cr renewal run-rate is exactly what the paper questions when it talks about high commissions on renewals.

Ditto sits differently. It's advice-led and doesn't depend on PoSP or dealer economics, so caps or disclosure should hurt it the least.

My read: PoSP (like Policybazaar, Turtlemint) and dealer-linked OEM brokers take the biggest hit. Direct online players, much less.

India’s power demand is rising, but the opportunity is not limited to power generation.

From generation to the grid, every stage needs massive investment.

Here’s a simple look at the opportunity 👇

1️⃣ ⚡ 𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡
𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆: ~₹18.5–19.5 lakh Cr investment during FY25–30

𝗡𝗧𝗣𝗖 | 𝗧𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 | 𝗕𝗛𝗘𝗟

India’s installed generation capacity is projected to reach ~874 GW by 2031–32.

2️⃣ 🔌 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗦𝗠𝗜𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗢𝗡
𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: >₹9.15 lakh Cr by 2032

𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗚𝗿𝗶𝗱 | 𝗞𝗘𝗖 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 | 𝗞𝗮𝗹𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘂 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 | 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹

Transmission network is planned to expand to 6.48 lakh ckm by 2032.

3️⃣ 🏗️ 𝗦𝗨𝗕𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦
𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗰𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆: 1,478 GVA → 2,345 GVA by 2032

𝗦𝗶𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 | 𝗚𝗘 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮 𝗧&𝗗 | 𝗛𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 | 𝗔𝗕𝗕

More substations will be required to connect new generation, renewables and rising industrial demand.

4️⃣ ⚙️ 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗦𝗙𝗢𝗥𝗠𝗘𝗥𝗦
𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁: ~US$4.1B in 2026 → ~US$5.5B by 2030

𝗖𝗚 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 | 𝗛𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 | 𝗩𝗼𝗹𝘁𝗮𝗺𝗽 | 𝗔𝘁𝗹𝗮𝗻𝘁𝗮 𝗘𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝘀

Transformers become increasingly critical as transmission capacity, renewables and data-centre demand expand.

5️⃣ 🔲 𝗦𝗪𝗜𝗧𝗖𝗛𝗚𝗘𝗔𝗥
𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁: ~US$5.8B in 2026 → ~US$8.2B by 2031

𝗔𝗕𝗕 | 𝗦𝗶𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 | 𝗖𝗚 𝗣𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 | 𝗛𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆

GIS, AIS and protection equipment are essential for reliable and safe power networks.

6️⃣ 🌐 𝗚𝗥𝗜𝗗 + 𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗚𝗬 𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗔𝗚𝗘
𝗕𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: ~₹3.49 lakh Cr by 2031–32
𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝗕𝗘𝗦𝗦: 47.24 GW / 236 GWh

𝗚𝗘 𝗩𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮 𝗧&𝗗 | 𝗛𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆 | 𝗔𝗕𝗕 | 𝗦𝗶𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗘𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗴𝘆

Grid modernisation, automation, storage and balancing will become increasingly important as renewable penetration rises.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚𝗚𝗘𝗥 𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘 👀

𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗲𝗿 → 𝗦𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗴𝗲𝗮𝗿 → 𝗚𝗿𝗶𝗱

This is why India’s power opportunity is much bigger than a single generation or transmission story.

The real opportunity is across the entire ecosystem—capacity addition, grid expansion, equipment replacement, renewable integration and energy storage. ⚡📊

India Weekly Market Review

September 21–25, 2026

Indian equities extended their losing streak to a seventh consecutive week. The Nifty 50 fell 0.88% to 23,140.50, while the Sensex declined 0.53% to 73,895.74. The Nifty has now fallen about 5.8% across seven straight weeks, its longest such losing run since the Covid-era sell-off. 

Sector performance

SectorWeekly move

Nifty Realty+3.0%
Nifty Consumer Durables+1.1%
Nifty Pharma+1.1%
Nifty FMCG+1.0%
Nifty India Defence+0.5%
Nifty Metal+0.3%
Nifty Oil & Gas-0.8%
Nifty Auto-0.6%
Nifty Private Bank-1.5%
Nifty IT-2.4%

The rotation was notable. Realty rebounded almost 3%, while pharma, consumer durables and FMCG held up relatively well. IT was the weakest major sector, followed by private banks and energy. 

Stock movers

The sharpest midcap sell-off came in PB Fintech, which plunged 33.1% for the week after IRDAI proposed changes to insurance-distribution economics. The proposed commission and expense changes raised concerns about the future earnings model of insurance intermediaries. 

Paytm and Oracle Financial Services Software each fell about 9.5%, while L&T Finance declined 9.2% and Container Corporation fell 8.5%. 

At the other end, Patanjali Foods gained about 10.1%, Mankind Pharma 7.6%, ICICI Lombard 6.6%, Phoenix Mills 5.4% and SAIL 4.3%. The moves were largely stock-specific rather than driven by a single broad market catalyst. 

Engineers India was another standout, gaining strongly after announcing a $450 million Dangote Group contract to provide project-management and EPCM services for a 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery and petrochemical project in Kenya. 

Welspun Corp also attracted attention after its US subsidiary won a $412.5 million HFIW pipe order, its largest such order, reinforcing the company's US infrastructure exposure. 

The macro backdrop

The week's biggest macro variables were oil, US yields and foreign flows.

Brent crude initially surged above $100 as Middle East tensions intensified, but prices subsequently fell sharply as hopes of renewed US-Iran negotiations and improved oil-flow conditions emerged. Brent ended the week around $97–98. 

The bigger pressure came from global bonds. The US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to around 5.19%, its highest level in years, keeping pressure on emerging-market assets and particularly rate-sensitive Indian equities. India's 10-year government bond yield also remained elevated. 

The Federal Reserve had raised rates to 3.75–4.00% the previous week, while its projections continued to leave the door open to another increase. The combination of higher US yields and a firm dollar remained a major headwind for foreign flows. 

The Bank of Japan also raised its policy rate to 1.25% on September 18, its highest level in 31 years. The move added another element to the global monetary-tightening story and reduced the attractiveness of Japan as an ultra-cheap funding source. 

The rupee, however, was relatively stable, ending at ₹95.82/$ versus ₹95.87 the previous Friday. 

Foreign investors remained the major source of selling pressure. FIIs sold ₹11,490 crore during the week, while DIIs bought ₹16,398 crore, providing a significant counterweight. 

The Mercator Take

The important development this week was not simply another fall in the Nifty. It was the continued divergence beneath the index.

Global liquidity remains tight, US yields are above 5%, foreign investors continue to withdraw capital and geopolitical uncertainty is keeping oil volatile. That combination is weighing disproportionately on IT, financials and other rate-sensitive areas.

Yet domestic liquidity is preventing a disorderly decline, while selected domestic sectors and company-specific stories are attracting buying interest.

When you plan to buy a high PE business, ask AI a much simpler question:

Stock A trades at 80x earnings. I expect a 15% CAGR return over the next 10 years. What earnings growth is required if:

1.  P/E stays at 80x
2. P/E derates to 60x
3. P/E derates to 40x (or its 10-year median)

Now comes the important part:

Can the business realistically deliver that required earnings growth?

This forces you to think about valuation and business fundamentals together.

You don't need a precise DCF to know when your investment thesis requires near perfect execution.

Bottom line:

India's position isn't shifting from a complete “no” to an unrestricted “yes.”

It's moving towards a conditional model: approved investment, local manufacturing and strategic safeguards.

This also connects to India's bigger industrial push.

Critical minerals supply the battery materials.

Semiconductors support vehicle electronics.

Auto PLI encourages domestic manufacturing.

The real opportunity lies in connecting these policies into one functioning supply chain.

Now consider the opportunity for Indian component makers.

More local EV manufacturing can create demand for batteries, motors, power electronics and specialised components.

Technology partnerships may help build capabilities that would otherwise take years to develop.

But incentives alone won't guarantee localisation.

But here's the important distinction.

Allowing Chinese investment doesn't automatically mean giving Chinese companies control.

India's approach remains focused on FDI approval, security checks and local manufacturing.

The objective is to access technology without creating fresh strategic vulnerabilities.

And India already has an example of this model.

JSW MG Motor India combines JSW Group with China's SAIC.

Tata AutoComp also has Chinese partnerships in EV drivetrains and automotive air-conditioning systems.

Such ventures show how Indian manufacturing and foreign technology can work together.

Think of two very different situations.

A Chinese company imports finished EVs into India.

Or it invests in an Indian factory, brings technology and builds a local supply chain.

The second creates manufacturing opportunities, but also raises questions around ownership and strategic dependence.

That's where the policy shift comes in.

On September 23, an official indicated that existing auto PLI applications involving Chinese investment may be considered if FDI approval is already in place.

India wants to manufacture more EVs locally.

But China has deep expertise in batteries, motors and power electronics.

Building a competitive EV ecosystem takes more than assembling cars.

It also requires access to the technology and components inside them.

First, why was the door closed?

Since 2020, investments from countries sharing India's land borders have required government approval.

BYD's proposed ~$1 billion EV factory was blocked, while Great Wall Motor's India plans stalled.

But India's EV ambitions created a difficult question.

India said no to Chinese carmakers. Now, the door is opening.

After years of blocking major Chinese auto investments, India may allow some Chinese-backed companies to access its Rs.25,938 crore auto PLI scheme.

What changed? And who stands to benefit? 👇

Adani’s Rs. 1.04 lakh CR Odisha Data Centre Park

Adani’s subsidiary High Density Data Centre has received approval for a 1 GW data centre at Naraj, with around 250 acres earmarked by Odisha. The proposed investment is ₹1.04 lakh crore

A 1 GW campus points toward very large-scale AI/cloud workloads, where GPU infrastructure, power availability, cooling, networking and low-latency connectivity become critical.

Alongside Adani, the state has cleared an Rs. 14,257 CR HCLTech AI-optimised data centre, a Rs. 22,634 CR Sentraforge AI campus/GCC, and another Rs. 1,500 CR data-centre project

Technology projects account for roughly Rs. 1.42 lakh CR of the Rs. 2.47 lakh CR investment pipeline recently approved

Odisha offers large land parcels and access to power infrastructure, while its coastal position can support connectivity/cable infrastructure. The state's own digital-economy plan is explicitly targeting data-centre development and plug-and-play parks.

A 1 GW data centre is essentially a huge electricity consumer. This strengthens the long-term case for renewable power, transmission, substations, transformers, cooling systems and battery/storage infrastructure around the data-centre buildout.

This Odisha project comes alongside its existing AdaniConneX presence and other planned centres, while the group has separately announced a major AI/data-centre project with Google in Andhra Pradesh.

📈Investment angle

A ₹1.04 lakh crore data-centre investment doesn't accrue only to the data-centre operator. It potentially creates demand across:

Power generation → transmission → transformers → electrical equipment → cooling → EPC → fibre/connectivity → servers → GPUs → networking → storage → cybersecurity.

Potential ecosystem names to track include Adani Enterprises/AdaniConneX, Power Grid, Hitachi Energy India, GE Vernova T&D, Siemens, ABB India, CG Power, BHEL, KEC International, Kalpataru Projects, RailTel, Tata Communications and Netweb—but the actual revenue exposure will differ materially by company.

ICRA estimates India's third-party data-centre capacity could reach 2,400–2,500 MW by FY28, with Rs. 90,000 CR of investment expected during FY26–FY28, highlighting the scale of the broader infrastructure cycle.

Need to watch: The key milestones will be land development, power availability, construction commencement, customer/GPU commitments, financing and phased commissioning.

WHAT TO STUDY BEFORE TAKING ANY DECISION
Just seeing strong growth or a good stock price performance is not enough.

Go through the company from multiple angles:
▪️ Balance Sheet — debt, net worth, cash, borrowings and overall financial strength
▪️ P&L Statement — revenue growth, margins, profitability and consistency
▪️ Cash Flow Statement — whether profits are actually converting into cash
▪️ Annual Report — business model, strategy, risks, subsidiaries and management commentary
▪️ Concall — management guidance, future plans, order book, capacity expansion and execution
▪️ Investor Presentation — business segments, customers, capacity, expansion plans and growth strategy
▪️ Exchange Announcements — orders, acquisitions, fund raising, contracts, new projects and other important developments
▪️ DRHP / RHP — particularly important for IPO-stage companies; understand the business, promoters, financials, objects of the issue and risk factors
▪️ Management & Promoters — background, track record, holding pattern, pledging and corporate governance
▪️ Order Book & Execution — size of order book, quality of orders and ability to convert them into revenue
▪️ Working Capital — receivables, inventory, payable days and cash conversion
▪️ Capacity Expansion — current capacity, utilisation and whether expansion is supported by actual demand
▪️ Customer Concentration — dependence on a few customers can increase business risk
▪️ Related Party Transactions — study them carefully
▪️ Debt & Interest Cost — understand how growth is being funded
▪️ Promoter Dilution / Fund Raising — track preferential issues, warrants, QIPs and other capital raising
▪️ Valuation — a good business can still demand careful valuation analysis
▪️ Execution — ultimately, management's ability to execute its stated plans matters the most

SME companies can offer interesting business models and growth opportunities, but they can also have higher execution, liquidity, governance and information risks, so deeper research is important rather than relying only on price action or social-media discussions.

Study the business first. Then study the numbers. Then study the management. Finally, study the valuation.

Quality Power: The Growth Story Looks Powerful. Here’s What Investors Need to Watch

₹1,945 crore.

That is the size of Quality Power Electrical Equipments’ consolidated order book at the end of Q1 FY27.

Nearly 1.9 times FY26 revenue.

The real question is much harder:

Can Quality Power convert this opportunity into sustained revenue growth, healthy margins, strong cash flow and high returns on the additional capital being deployed?

That is where the next phase of the story gets interesting.

1. First, Look at What Happened in Q1 FY27

Quality Power delivered revenue of ₹256.4 crore, up 32% YoY.

But the more interesting numbers were underneath the revenue growth.

Gross margin improved from 44.6% to 47.2%.

Reported EBITDA was ₹64.7 crore, giving a 25.2% margin.

More importantly, after excluding the ₹7.82 crore non-cash Ind-AS 29 monetary loss related to its Turkish operations, EBITDA was ₹72.5 crore, translating into a 28.3% margin.

Adjusted PAT was ₹54.5 crore.

So, roughly speaking:

Revenue grew 32%

while

adjusted EBITDA grew almost 50%.

That is the first clue.

The business is not merely getting bigger.

It is beginning to show operating leverage and better mix.

Investor Takeaway

Q1 FY27 provides early evidence that the enlarged Quality Power platform is generating operating leverage. However, the 28.3% adjusted EBITDA margin should not be simply annualised, because the company is entering a significant commissioning and capacity-expansion phase.

2. But Don't Annualise That 28% EBITDA Margin

This is where retail investors can easily get carried away.

A 28.3% adjusted EBITDA margin in Q1 looks extremely attractive.

But management itself is not asking investors to assume that margin will continue.

Why?

Because Quality Power is entering a heavy commissioning phase.

The new Sangli facility will bring additional:

depreciation
manpower costs
power costs
factory overheads
qualification expenses.

These costs will hit the P&L before the new capacity reaches full utilization.

Management therefore expects some margin moderation, particularly around Q3, before utilization improves over the following 15 months.

Q1 margin tells us what the existing business can earn.

FY27 margins will tell us what happens when the company invests ahead of demand.

That is a much more important test.

Investor Takeaway

The more useful number to monitor is not whether Quality Power can maintain 28% EBITDA margins every quarter, but whether it can maintain approximately high-teens/20% margins during the expansion phase and subsequently recover margins as utilization increases.

3. The ₹1,945 Crore Order Book Changes the Conversation

At June 30, Quality Power had a consolidated order book of:

₹1,945 crore

Approximately 1.9× FY26 revenue.

And it is not concentrated in one business.

Endoks: ~₹801 crore

Mehru: ~₹585 crore

Quality Power: ~₹553 crore.

That provides substantial visibility.

But there is an important lesson for investors:

An order book is an opportunity, not an earnings number.

The company still has to manufacture, qualify, deliver and collect.

And Quality Power is doing all of this while simultaneously commissioning new capacity.

So the next phase is really an execution story.

Investor Takeaway

The ₹1,945 crore order book provides strong revenue visibility. But investors should now shift their attention from order-book size to order-book conversion, execution timelines, margins and cash generation.

4. And the Quality of the Orders Is Becoming Interesting

During Q1, Quality Power received major orders including:

₹48.3 crore of high-voltage reactors for a US data-centre project.

₹40.9 crore FACTS-related order for Japan.

₹15.7 crore order for 400 kV instrument transformers from Hitachi Energy India.

Notice the themes.

This isn't simply about conventional electrical equipment.

The company is increasingly participating in:

HVDC + FACTS + grid modernization + renewable integration + data-centre infrastructure + energy storage.

These are areas where power infrastructure is becoming increasingly technically demanding.

And that matters because the competitive advantage in such businesses is not necessarily just manufacturing capacity.

It is also:

technology + qualification + customer references + engineering capability.

Investor Takeaway

The opportunity is becoming broader and more technically differentiated. Investors should track order intake by product and geography, rather than looking only at the total order-book number.

5. This Is Where Quality Power's Story Gets Much More Interesting

Think about how a new entrant would compete with Quality Power.

It isn't enough to build a factory.

For high-voltage equipment, customers need:

Factory → testing → certification → customer audit → qualification → reference orders.

Quality Power is now going through extensive audits and qualification exercises with global OEMs and utilities.

The new Sangli facility alone is expected to undergo around 60 customer audits as the company prepares to move orders into the new facility.

That creates a potential barrier to entry.

And it explains why the company's investments in engineering, testing and customer qualification may be more important than simply looking at installed capacity.

Investor Takeaway

The potential moat is increasingly about qualification + technology + customer references + engineering capability, rather than manufacturing capacity alone.

6. Sangli Could Become the Next Major Inflection Point

The new Sangli facility is not just another factory.

Management believes it can ultimately support approximately ₹1,500–1,800 crore of revenue capacity.

But don't interpret that as immediate revenue.

There is a qualification process.

Trial production has to happen.

Customers have to approve the facility.

Orders have to migrate.

Utilization has to build.

And only then does the installed capacity translate into revenue and profits.

This creates an interesting situation.

Today: Orders exist.

Tomorrow: Capacity becomes available.

Later: Utilization determines profitability.

That last step is where the real operating leverage can emerge.

Investor Takeaway

Sangli could materially increase Quality Power's revenue ceiling, but FY27 should be viewed as a commissioning, qualification and ramp-up phase rather than a full-capacity year.

7. Quality Power Is Also Moving Deeper Into the HVDC Value Chain

The company is commissioning a High Voltage CTC Magnet Wire facility.

Why is this important?

Because Quality Power is increasingly positioning itself around the HVDC ecosystem.

Backward integration into a critical input can potentially provide:

better supply security
greater control over quality
participation in larger HVDC programs
potential cost and margin benefits.

But this is still an emerging capability.

Management expects trial runs over several months, with full production around Q4 FY27.

So this is future optionality, not something investors should already capitalise aggressively into earnings.

Investor Takeaway

The CTC magnet-wire facility could deepen Quality Power's participation in the HVDC value chain. But investors should wait for production, qualification, customer acceptance and actual financial contribution before assigning substantial value to this opportunity.

8. Then There Is Endoks
This could quietly become one of the most important pieces of the Quality Power story.

Endoks already has approximately:

₹801 crore of order book

Its portfolio includes:

STATCOM
SVC
harmonic filters
automation
BESS power conversion systems.

Management indicated that traditional power-electronics products such as STATCOM/SVC/automation can generate around 25% margins.

But BESS is potentially much more interesting.

The company has indicated around US$60 million of BESS PCS orders/pipeline, with the possibility of another US$40 million over the following 12 months.

And BESS projects have relatively short execution cycles of approximately 6–9 months.

So Endoks could potentially provide Quality Power with something very valuable:
a faster-growing business sitting alongside its traditional grid infrastructure business.

But again, the key question is not the size of the opportunity.
It is:
What margins and cash returns will BESS ultimately generate?

Investor Takeaway

Endoks and BESS could become important incremental growth engines. But BESS should currently be viewed as emerging opportunity rather than established earnings power until shipments, margins and cash generation are demonstrated.

9. Mehru Is Another Piece of the Puzzle

Mehru was acquired as a turnaround opportunity.

The company is now focusing on:
improving throughput
reducing changeover time
improving material flow
removing bottlenecks
increasing utilization of existing assets.

Management is targeting around 18% EBITDA margin going forward.

This is important because Quality Power is increasingly trying to create growth without simply throwing more capital at every problem.

The idea is:

First improve utilization of what you already own.
That can produce much better incremental returns than continuously building new factories.

Investor Takeaway
Mehru is an important test of Quality Power's ability to turn acquisitions into higher utilization, better margins and stronger returns, rather than simply adding revenue.

10. But There Is One Number Investors Should Not Ignore: Cash Flow

FY26 EBITDA was around:

₹236 crore

But operating cash flow was only around:

₹80 crore

So cash conversion was approximately:

0.3× EBITDA

And this ratio has declined over the last few years.

That doesn't mean the accounting profits are wrong.

It means that rapid growth is consuming cash through working capital and expansion.

And this is exactly why investors need to watch:

Receivables
Inventory
Working capital
Operating cash flow

as closely as they watch EBITDA.

Because ultimately:

₹100 of EBITDA is much more valuable when it becomes ₹80–90 of cash than when it remains tied up in working capital.

Investor Takeaway

Cash conversion is one of the most important areas to monitor. The next leg of the thesis becomes much stronger if CFO begins catching up with EBITDA rather than remaining structurally weak.

11. The Balance Sheet, However, Gives the Company Considerable Room

Quality Power's FY26 debt/equity was only around:

0.05×

That is a very low level of leverage for a company undergoing this degree of expansion.

So debt is currently not the biggest concern.

Instead, the question is:

How efficiently will management deploy capital from here?

And that question has become much more important after the latest announcement.

Investor Takeaway

Financial leverage currently provides a cushion. The bigger issue has shifted from balance-sheet risk to capital-allocation risk.

12. Enter Winwin

On September 23, Quality Power announced an agreement to acquire up to 100% of Winwin Speciality Insulators.

The proposed consideration is up to:

₹272.34 crore

of which up to:

₹123.84 crore is cash

and the balance is through equity shares.

Quality Power proposes to issue up to 10.17 lakh shares at ₹1,460 per share to certain selling shareholders.

What does Winwin bring?

High-voltage:
ceramic insulators
polymeric insulators
transmission equipment capability.

Strategically, it fits.

It operates in the same broad power-transmission ecosystem.

It could help Quality Power create a more integrated offering.

But here is the part investors should notice.

Winwin's revenue was only approximately:

₹1.07 crore in FY24

₹12.72 crore in FY25

₹17.07 crore in FY26.

So the acquisition is not being justified by current revenue alone.

The investment thesis depends on what happens next:
capacity utilization + exports + cross-selling + integration + operating leverage.
That makes Winwin a capital-allocation test.

Investor Takeaway

Strategically, Winwin fits the broader transmission ecosystem. Financially, however, investors need to see how the acquisition scales from its current revenue base and what return Quality Power ultimately earns on the capital committed.

13. And Then Came the ₹700 Crore QIP

On September 23, the Board also approved a proposal to raise up to:

₹700 crore through QIP

subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals.

This is a significant development.

Quality Power is effectively saying:

We see enough opportunities to deploy substantial additional capital, but we want to preserve a relatively low-leverage balance sheet while doing it.

That has two sides.

Positive:

The company gets capital to accelerate growth.

Watchpoint:

Existing shareholders also need to think about dilution.

Therefore, the question becomes:

How much incremental EBITDA and free cash flow will the company generate from every ₹100 crore of new equity capital?

That is the number I would want to see over the next few years.

Investor Takeaway

The QIP should not be viewed simply as positive or negative. The important question is whether fresh equity capital produces attractive incremental earnings and cash flow per share.

14. This Is Why ROCE Becomes More Important Than Revenue Growth

FY26 ROCE was approximately:

39.8%

ROE was:

26.6%

Those are strong numbers.

But the past ROCE was generated on the existing asset base.

The company is now investing heavily in:

Sangli

CTC magnet wire

Endoks

Mehru

GIS

Winwin

international expansion.

The real test is therefore:

Can the next ₹500–1,000 crore of capital earn returns anywhere close to the returns generated by the existing business?

That is far more important than whether revenue grows 20%, 25% or 30%.

Investor Takeaway

Historical ROCE establishes that the existing business is capable of generating attractive returns. The next phase will test incremental ROCE, which is the more relevant measure for a rapidly expanding company.

15. What Investors Are Really Buying Now

The easy part of the Quality Power story is becoming increasingly visible:

Large order book
↓
Strong revenue visibility
↓
New manufacturing capacity
↓
Multiple growth engines

↓

Expanding product portfolio

But the harder part starts from here.

The company is simultaneously taking on:

More capacity

More acquisitions

More products

More geographies

More capital

And that changes the questions investors need to ask.

Earlier, the key question was:

Is there enough demand for Quality Power's products?

The ₹1,945 crore order book provides considerable evidence that demand exists.

Now the questions become:

Can the ₹1,945 crore order book be converted into revenue on schedule?

Can the new Sangli capacity be commissioned and qualified without significant delays?

Can EBITDA margins remain around the high-teens/20% level as new capacity comes on stream?

Can working capital convert a greater proportion of EBITDA into cash?

Can acquisitions such as Winwin generate attractive returns on the capital invested?

And most importantly:

Can the next phase of growth generate returns on incremental capital that are anywhere close to the company's existing ROCE?

That is the crucial transition.

Quality Power is moving from a business where growth itself was the primary attraction to one where the quality of incremental growth will determine the outcome.

Investor Takeaway

The investment thesis has evolved from “Can Quality Power grow?” to “Can Quality Power grow efficiently?”

16. The Quality Power Scorecard Investors Should Now Track

Forget trying to predict the share price every quarter.

Watch these six things instead.

1. Revenue Growth

Can the company sustain approximately 20%+ growth after the acquisition-led FY26 jump?

2. EBITDA Margin

Does the margin settle around management's indicated high-teens/20% range and then recover as new capacity gets utilized?

3. Order-Book Conversion

Can the ₹1,945 crore order book actually translate into revenue on schedule?

4. Cash Conversion

Does CFO begin catching up with EBITDA?

5. Incremental ROCE

Does new capacity and acquisition capital generate attractive returns?

6. Acquisition Discipline

Does Winwin become a meaningful contributor, or does it remain a capital-heavy asset that takes years to scale?

Investor Takeaway

These six indicators will tell investors much more than simply tracking quarterly revenue or PAT growth.

The Bottom Line

Quality Power has moved beyond being a simple electrical equipment manufacturer.

It is attempting to build a global high-voltage and power-technology platform spanning transmission, HVDC, FACTS, power quality, energy storage and adjacent equipment.

The existing business already demonstrates some attractive characteristics:

High ROCE

Low leverage

Strong margins

Large order visibility

Technology-led products

International customers

The next phase, however, will be defined by capital allocation and execution.

Sangli has to ramp.

BESS has to scale.

Mehru has to improve.

Winwin has to justify its acquisition cost.

The QIP capital has to earn attractive returns.

And most importantly, EBITDA needs to increasingly translate into cash.

That is what makes Quality Power interesting from here.

The first chapter was about building the business.

The second chapter was about scaling it through acquisitions and capacity.

The next chapter is about something investors should care about even more:

Can management turn a ₹1,945 crore opportunity pipeline and a much larger capital base into sustained earnings, cash flow and high incremental returns?

That is the Quality Power story to watch through FY27–FY29.

How much of an NBFC's and bank's profit rides on selling insurance?

Start with NBFCs. Insurance commission income now eats into profit before tax at levels that should worry anyone tracking these stocks.

L&T Finance is the standout at 25.6% of PBT, and analysts at Macquarie flag it as the most exposed name in the sector, followed by Piramal Enterprises and Cholamandalam Investment and Finance. Poonawalla Fincorp sits at 17.8%, Cholamandalam at 16.3%. Even HDB Financial, M&M Financial, and CreditAccess Grameen hover around 13%.

If the cap forces a 50% cut in this income, L&T Finance alone could lose roughly 13% of its PBT.

Now look at banks through a slightly different lens, bancassurance income as a share of total fee income for FY26. Bandhan Bank tops the list at 26.4%, way ahead of everyone else. HDFC Bank pulls in ₹6,927 crore from this, 16.9% of its fee income. Axis Bank is at 15.1%, IndusInd at 15.5%, Yes Bank at 14.9%. 

Private banks as a group get 12.4% of fee income from bancassurance, more than double the PSU bank average of 6%. Foreign banks land in between at 8.6%, largely driven by Standard Chartered at 13.6%.

That's why analysts specifically called out Axis Bank and HDFC Bank as more exposed among private lenders, simply because fee income and PBT lean harder on this line for them than for peers.

Then there's the second table, insurance commission as % of PBT for specific financiers. L&T Finance again leads at 0.26, more than triple Poonawalla Fincorp's 0.18. Among vehicle financiers, Cholamandalam Investment and Finance sits at 0.16 versus Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services at 0.13. Bajaj Finance and Tata Capital are both a modest 0.08, Aditya Birla Finance lowest at 0.04.

The Legend of Willy Jeep , From Toledo to the Indian Army  🚙

#IndianArmy #WillysJeep #MilitaryHistory #ADGPI 

📌The Willys MB (and the almost identical Ford GPW) was built in the United States in 1941 as a light reconnaissance vehicle: about a quarter-ton, four-wheel drive, a 60 hp “Go-Devil” engine, and a body that could be repaired with a spanner in a ditch. Allied commanders later ranked it among the tools that mattered most in the Second World War. General George C. Marshall called it “America’s greatest contribution to modern warfare.” War correspondent Ernie Pyle wrote that it went everywhere and was “as faithful as a dog, as strong as a mule and as agile as a goat.

📌Jeeps reached 🇮🇳 during the Burma  🇲🇲 and Kohima campaigns. After 1947 they stayed. Mahindra & Mahindra won a licence to assemble Willys kits and later built the high-bonnet CJ-3B, the machine most Indians still mean when they say “Willys” or “army jeep.” The Indian Army used these jeeps (and later the Nissan Jonga) into the 1980s as command cars, ambulances, and, crucially, mounts for the 106 mm recoilless rifle

📌The story that turned the jeep into legend is the Battle of Asal Uttar (8–10 September 1965), in the Khem Karan sector of Punjab — the largest tank battle in the subcontinent since the Second World War.
